questions.text: Is the appliance firmware up to date?
questions.description: Running outdated firmware on a Forcepoint appliance exposes the system to known vulnerabilities patched in subsequent releases. Firmware currency is also a prerequisite for TAC support on production issues.
questions.remediation:
Log in to the appliance management interface and navigate to the firmware/system update section. Compare the installed version against the latest release on support.forcepoint.com for the relevant appliance model. Apply the current firmware during a scheduled maintenance window and review release notes for known issues before upgrading.

Forcepoint KB: 'How to upgrade firmware on Forcepoint appliances' — refer to the Hardware Appliance Installation Guide for your model.

questions.text: Are hardware diagnostics showing any errors?
questions.description: Hardware diagnostic errors (disk failures, memory faults, NIC errors, RAID degradation) are early indicators of imminent hardware failure. Ignoring these alerts can result in unplanned outages, data loss, or silent data corruption that degrades security inspection quality without visible symptoms.
questions.remediation:
Access the appliance hardware diagnostic interface (IPMI/iDRAC/iLO) and review the System Event Log (SEL) for error entries. Identify the failing component and engage Forcepoint TAC or the hardware vendor for RMA if within warranty. For RAID degradation, initiate a rebuild immediately.

Forcepoint KB: Contact Forcepoint TAC (support.forcepoint.com) with the SEL dump and appliance serial number for hardware RMA initiation.

questions.text: Is the appliance running on supported hardware?
questions.description: Running Forcepoint software on hardware not listed in the official Hardware Compatibility List (HCL) or that has reached End-of-Hardware-Support means the configuration is unsupported by TAC. Performance characteristics may differ from tested configurations and hardware-specific optimisations in the software may not function correctly.
questions.remediation:
Verify the appliance model and specifications against the Forcepoint Hardware Compatibility List on support.forcepoint.com. If the hardware is not listed or has reached End-of-Support, engage account management to initiate a hardware refresh discussion.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to 'Forcepoint Appliance Hardware Compatibility List' and End-of-Sale/End-of-Life announcements on support.forcepoint.com.

questions.text: Are power supplies redundant and functional?
questions.description: A single power supply failure in a non-redundant or degraded PSU configuration will cause an unplanned appliance outage. Even where a second PSU is present, a failed secondary PSU leaves the system with no power redundancy — making any subsequent electrical event a single point of failure.
questions.remediation:
Physically inspect or use IPMI/management console to verify PSU status on all installed power supplies. Replace any failed or degraded PSU within the hardware warranty. Verify that both PSUs are connected to separate PDUs or circuits for maximum resilience.

Forcepoint KB: Consult the Hardware Appliance Installation Guide for PSU replacement procedures. Engage Forcepoint TAC or authorised hardware partner for PSU RMA under warranty.

questions.text: Is storage capacity within acceptable limits (<80%)?
questions.description: Storage utilisation above 80% on an appliance running Forcepoint software risks critical service disruptions. Log Server, database services, and temporary file storage can all fail when disk capacity is exhausted. Full disk conditions are a well-documented root cause of Forcepoint service crashes, log gaps, and database corruption.
questions.remediation:
Review disk utilisation using df -h on the appliance. Identify partitions approaching capacity — commonly /var, /opt, or database partitions. Archive or purge old logs per the retention policy. For persistent capacity issues, evaluate storage expansion options.

Forcepoint KB: 'Disk space management on Forcepoint appliances' — contact TAC for guidance on safely removing old logs and temporary files. Monitor storage with automated alerting at 75% and 85% thresholds.

questions.description: Non-operational cooling fans cause CPU and component temperatures to rise above safe thresholds, leading to thermal throttling, automatic shutdown, or permanent hardware damage. In high-ambient-temperature environments (Middle East data centres), fan failures can cause hardware damage within hours.
questions.remediation:
Check fan status via the appliance IPMI/management interface or hardware diagnostics page. Replace any failed or below-threshold-RPM fans immediately. Verify that the appliance rack has adequate airflow and that hot aisle/cold aisle containment is properly implemented.

Forcepoint KB: Engage Forcepoint TAC or the hardware maintenance partner for fan replacement under warranty. Refer to the appliance Hardware Maintenance Manual for FRU procedures.

questions.description: Expired hardware warranty means hardware failures (failed disks, PSUs, NICs, CPUs) will not be covered by vendor replacement, resulting in costly out-of-warranty repairs or unplanned hardware procurement. During warranty, Forcepoint and hardware partners guarantee next-business-day or same-day replacement for critical components.
questions.remediation:
Verify the warranty expiry date for each appliance using the serial number on the hardware vendor's warranty lookup portal or via Forcepoint account management. Engage procurement to initiate hardware refresh or extended warranty renewal before expiry.

Forcepoint KB: Contact your Forcepoint account manager or partner for hardware refresh options. For Forcepoint-branded appliances, check entitlement on the Forcepoint customer portal.

questions.description: Forcepoint appliances that have reached End-of-Sale (EoS) are on a defined timeline toward End-of-Support (EoL), after which security patches, software updates, and TAC support will no longer be available. Continuing to operate EoS hardware creates a growing security debt and compliance risk.
questions.remediation:
Cross-reference all appliance models against Forcepoint's published End-of-Sale/End-of-Life announcements on support.forcepoint.com. For any appliance that has reached EoS, initiate a hardware refresh planning project with defined replacement dates before the EoL date.

Forcepoint KB: 'Forcepoint Product End-of-Life Policy' on support.forcepoint.com. Contact your Forcepoint SE for migration assistance.

questions.text: Are all network interfaces properly configured?
questions.description: Misconfigured network interfaces — incorrect IP addresses, wrong subnet masks, duplex/speed mismatches, or disabled interfaces — can cause partial or complete loss of traffic inspection, management connectivity, or inter-component communication. Interface misconfigurations are a frequent root cause of intermittent proxy failures.
questions.remediation:
Review network interface configuration on the appliance using the management console or CLI (ip addr, ifconfig, ethtool). Verify that each interface has the correct IP, subnet, and gateway. Confirm duplex and speed settings match the connected switch port. Validate that all expected interfaces are in UP state.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Network Configuration Guide. For complex networking issues, engage Forcepoint TAC with a network diagram and interface configuration dump.

questions.description: Network bonding or teaming provides link aggregation and redundancy. A misconfigured bond (wrong bonding mode, mismatched LACP settings on the switch, or a failed member interface) can result in reduced throughput, intermittent connectivity loss, or complete failure of the bond interface.
questions.remediation:
Review the bonding configuration using cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0 (or equivalent) and verify all member interfaces are active. Confirm that the bonding mode (LACP/802.3ad, active-backup) matches the switch port channel configuration. Verify switch-side port-channel status to ensure LACP negotiation is successful.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Deployment Guide for bonding configuration requirements. Engage your network team to verify switch-side LACP configuration.

questions.text: Are VLANs configured as per network design?
questions.description: VLANs that are incorrectly tagged, missing, or applied to the wrong interfaces can cause traffic segregation failures — allowing traffic from different security zones to mix, preventing management access, or causing monitoring traffic to be misdirected. VLAN misconfiguration is a common cause of unexplained connectivity issues.
questions.remediation:
Review VLAN configuration on the appliance and compare against the approved network design documentation. Verify that 802.1Q trunk interfaces are receiving the correct VLAN tags from the connected switch. Confirm that management, production, and monitoring VLANs are correctly separated.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Deployment Guide for VLAN interface configuration. Engage your network team to verify switch trunk/access port configuration.

questions.description: Network throughput degradation on an appliance interface — due to duplex mismatch, cable issues, switch port errors, or NIC faults — directly reduces the volume of traffic that can be inspected. Interface errors and drops are a common but underdiagnosed performance problem in Forcepoint deployments.
questions.remediation:
Check interface error counters using ifconfig or ip -s link on the appliance. High values for RX errors, TX errors, or dropped packets indicate an interface-level problem. Common causes include duplex mismatch, faulty SFP/cable, or a failing NIC. Replace faulty hardware and resolve duplex/speed mismatches.

Forcepoint KB: 'Troubleshooting network interface performance on Forcepoint appliances' — engage TAC with interface statistics and the network topology for diagnosis.

questions.description: Incorrect routing table entries on the appliance can cause traffic to be sent to the wrong next-hop, preventing the appliance from communicating with update servers, management systems, LDAP directories, or SIEM platforms. Routing misconfigurations are particularly impactful in multi-interface deployments.
questions.remediation:
Review the appliance routing table using ip route or route -n. Verify that the default gateway is correct and reachable. Confirm that static routes required for management network, update server, or LDAP/AD connectivity are present. Test reachability using ping and traceroute from the appliance.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Network Configuration Guide for static route configuration syntax.

questions.description: DNS resolution failures on the appliance affect the product's ability to resolve update server hostnames (downloads.websense.com, updates.forcepoint.com), LDAP/AD server names, and external threat intelligence sources. Failed DNS lookups can halt database updates and break authentication integrations.
questions.remediation:
Test DNS resolution from the appliance using nslookup or dig for critical hostnames. Verify that the configured DNS server IPs in /etc/resolv.conf are correct and reachable. Confirm that DNS servers can resolve both internal (AD) and external (update server) hostnames. If using split DNS, verify that the correct DNS server is configured for each zone.

Forcepoint KB: 'DNS configuration requirements for Forcepoint appliances and services' — refer to the Forcepoint system requirements documentation.

questions.text: Are static routes documented and verified?
questions.description: Undocumented static routes on the appliance create operational risk: routes added to resolve temporary issues are often forgotten and can conflict with future network changes. In security appliances, incorrect routing can cause traffic to bypass inspection or reach unintended networks.
questions.remediation:
Export and review all static routes configured on the appliance. For each route, verify it has a documented business justification and was added through the change management process. Remove any routes that are no longer required. Ensure the appliance routing configuration is included in the CMDB.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the change management process for appliance configuration changes. Store the approved routing configuration in the CMDB.

questions.text: Is network latency within acceptable range?
questions.description: Elevated network latency between the appliance and critical infrastructure (AD servers, log servers, database servers) degrades product performance and can cause authentication timeouts, log processing delays, and database write failures. In proxy deployments, latency to DNS resolvers directly contributes to user-facing page load times.
questions.remediation:
Measure round-trip latency from the appliance to critical infrastructure using ping and MTR. Identify any network paths with consistently high latency (>5ms for LAN). Investigate causes: congested links, suboptimal routing, or overloaded infrastructure. Engage the network team to optimise paths for performance-critical communications.

Forcepoint KB: 'Performance baselines and network requirements for Forcepoint deployments' — engage Forcepoint TAC or Professional Services if latency-related performance issues are impacting product services.

questions.text: Is CPU usage within acceptable limits (<80%)?
questions.description: CPU utilisation above 80% on an appliance indicates the system is operating near capacity, leading to increased processing latency, request queuing, and risk of service failure under traffic spikes. Forcepoint services (proxy, DLP scanning, firewall inspection) are CPU-intensive; sustained high CPU is a primary indicator of undersized or overloaded hardware.
questions.remediation:
Identify the top CPU-consuming processes using top or ps aux on the appliance. Determine whether the load is from a Forcepoint service process or an OS-level process. For Forcepoint service CPU overload, review throughput against the appliance's rated capacity and consider adding additional nodes.

Forcepoint KB: 'CPU utilisation troubleshooting on Forcepoint appliances' — engage TAC with a top output snapshot and performance logs if CPU is consistently above 80%.

questions.text: Is memory utilization within normal range (<85%)?
questions.description: Memory utilisation above 85% on a Forcepoint appliance risks system instability, process crashes, and OOM (Out of Memory) killer events that can terminate critical Forcepoint service processes. High memory conditions are particularly common when log databases, content caches, or in-memory classification engines are not tuned to available RAM.
questions.remediation:
Review memory utilisation using free -h and /proc/meminfo on the appliance. Identify top memory consumers using ps aux --sort=-%mem. Tune memory limits for Forcepoint service processes where applicable. If memory is consistently above 85% with properly tuned services, the appliance is undersized for the workload.

Forcepoint KB: 'Memory tuning and troubleshooting guide for Forcepoint appliances' — engage TAC for product-specific memory tuning guidance.

questions.text: Are disk I/O operations performing adequately?
questions.description: Poor disk I/O performance on the appliance directly affects log writing, database operations, content caching, and temporary file handling. High I/O wait is a common cause of proxy slowness, log gaps, and database timeouts in Forcepoint deployments. Disk I/O bottlenecks often precede full disk failures.
questions.remediation:
Use iostat -x 1 10 to review disk I/O statistics. Look for high %iowait and high await (average I/O wait time >20ms). Identify processes generating the highest I/O using iotop. For spinning disk systems, consider migrating database and log partitions to SSD. Check SMART data for disk health indicators using smartctl.

Forcepoint KB: 'Disk I/O performance troubleshooting on Forcepoint appliances' — engage TAC with iostat output and disk health data if I/O issues are causing service degradation.

questions.description: Suboptimal network throughput on the appliance can result from NIC configuration issues, insufficient network buffer sizes, or interrupt coalescing settings not tuned for the traffic volume. Unoptimised network settings can limit the appliance's ability to process traffic at line rate, creating inspection bottlenecks.
questions.remediation:
Review NIC configuration using ethtool for ring buffer sizes, interrupt coalescing settings, and offload capabilities (TSO, GRO, LRO). For high-throughput deployments, tune ring buffer sizes and consider increasing CPU interrupt affinities. Benchmark throughput against the appliance's rated capacity.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Performance Tuning Guide. Engage TAC for NIC-specific tuning recommendations.

questions.description: Without documented performance baselines, it is impossible to determine whether current appliance performance metrics represent normal operation or degradation. Baselines are essential for capacity planning, detecting slow performance regressions, and justifying hardware refresh decisions to management.
questions.remediation:
Establish performance baselines by recording CPU, memory, disk I/O, network throughput, and key application metrics during a representative business day. Store baselines in a monitoring system or operations runbook. Review baselines quarterly and after any significant configuration change.

Forcepoint KB: Engage Forcepoint Professional Services to establish performance baselines as part of a Health Check engagement.

questions.text: Is load balancing configured and working?
questions.description: In multi-appliance deployments, the absence of properly configured load balancing results in uneven traffic distribution, overloading individual appliances while others remain underutilised. A single appliance failure in such a scenario causes a disproportionate impact on the remaining nodes.
questions.remediation:
Review the load balancing configuration for the appliance cluster. Verify that traffic is distributed evenly across nodes by comparing transaction rates and resource utilisation. Configure load balancer health checks to automatically remove failed appliances from the pool. Test failover by simulating an appliance failure.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Deployment Guide for clustering and load balancing architecture guidance.

questions.description: Without configured performance alerts, appliance resource saturation (CPU, memory, disk, network) goes undetected until it causes a service outage. Proactive alerting enables the operations team to address resource pressure before it impacts users or causes security events to be missed.
questions.remediation:
Configure SNMP traps or syslog-based alerting for key performance thresholds: CPU >75%, memory >80%, disk >75%, and interface error rate above baseline. Integrate alerts into the NOC monitoring platform (Zabbix, PRTG, Nagios, or SIEM). Test alert delivery by simulating threshold breaches.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance SNMP MIB documentation for available OIDs to monitor.

questions.description: Unoptimised connection pooling in Forcepoint proxy and database-connected services leads to excessive connection establishment overhead, database connection exhaustion, and suboptimal resource utilisation. In high-transaction environments, connection pool sizing directly affects throughput and latency.
questions.remediation:
Review connection pool configuration for the applicable Forcepoint service (Content Gateway database connections, Log Server database pool, DLP manager connections). Adjust pool sizes based on observed peak concurrent connection counts. Ensure idle connection timeout settings prevent pool exhaustion from stale connections.

Forcepoint KB: Engage Forcepoint TAC for product-specific connection pool tuning guidance.

questions.text: Is management access secured with strong authentication?
questions.description: Weak or default authentication for appliance management access is a critical security risk. Attackers who gain management access to a Forcepoint appliance can disable security policies, exfiltrate logs, or use the appliance as a pivot point within the network. Management interfaces without strong authentication are a common target in lateral movement attacks.
questions.remediation:
Enforce strong password policies for all management accounts. Disable default credentials immediately after initial setup. Enable MFA for management console access where supported. Restrict management access to a dedicated management network or VPN.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Security Hardening Guide for management interface security best practices.

questions.text: Are administrative accounts following least privilege?
questions.description: Administrative accounts with excessive privileges violate the least privilege principle. Compromised or misused high-privilege accounts can cause irreversible configuration changes, policy bypasses, or data exfiltration from the appliance.
questions.remediation:
Review all administrative accounts in the Forcepoint management console and the appliance OS. Apply role-based access control: assign read-only, operator, and administrator roles based on job function. Ensure no shared administrator accounts exist. Implement a privileged access management (PAM) solution.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Administrator Guide for role-based access control configuration.

questions.description: Password-based SSH authentication is vulnerable to brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and password reuse exploits. Without SSH key-based authentication, the appliance management interface is exposed to authentication attacks that may succeed if password policies are insufficient.
questions.remediation:
Generate SSH key pairs for all administrators requiring SSH access. Deploy public keys to the appliance's authorized_keys file. Disable password-based SSH authentication in sshd_config (PasswordAuthentication no). Restrict SSH access to specific source IP addresses using firewall rules.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Security Hardening Guide for SSH configuration recommendations.

questions.text: Are security patches up to date?
questions.description: Unpatched security vulnerabilities in the appliance OS and installed packages can be exploited by attackers to gain elevated access, install persistent backdoors, or disrupt appliance services. CVEs affecting common Linux components (OpenSSL, glibc, kernel) are regularly exploited in targeted attacks against security infrastructure.
questions.remediation:
Review installed OS package versions against current CVE databases and Forcepoint security advisories. Apply OS security patches during scheduled maintenance windows following the patch management policy. For Forcepoint-managed appliances, check the support portal for approved patch bundles. Test patches in non-production before production deployment.

Forcepoint KB: Subscribe to Forcepoint Security Advisories on support.forcepoint.com. Review Forcepoint Appliance patching guidance — not all OS patches are applicable without Forcepoint validation.

questions.text: Is audit logging enabled and retained?
questions.description: Without audit logging enabled and retained, administrative actions on the appliance (configuration changes, policy modifications, user account changes) cannot be reviewed, correlated with security events, or used for forensic investigation. Regulatory frameworks including ISO 27001, PCI-DSS, and GDPR require audit trails for privileged access.
questions.remediation:
Enable audit logging (auditd) on the appliance OS and configure rules to capture administrative actions, privilege escalation events, and file system changes in sensitive configuration directories. Configure log forwarding to a centralised syslog server or SIEM. Set log retention to meet compliance requirements (minimum 1 year for most frameworks).

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Security Hardening Guide for audit logging configuration.

questions.description: Unused and unnecessary services running on the appliance expand the attack surface. Each enabled service represents a potential exploitation vector. Default appliance builds often include services not required for the specific deployment role, which should be disabled as part of security hardening.
questions.remediation:
Review all running services on the appliance using systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running. Identify services not required for the appliance's operational role. Disable and mask unnecessary services. Document the approved service list and verify against it during maintenance reviews.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Security Hardening Guide for the approved service configuration. Do not disable services without confirming with Forcepoint TAC that they are not required for product functionality.

questions.description: SNMP v1 and v2c use community strings transmitted in cleartext, making them vulnerable to network sniffing attacks. An attacker who obtains the SNMP community string can query sensitive device information and in some configurations make configuration changes. SNMP v3 provides authentication and encryption and should be the only enabled version.
questions.remediation:
Disable SNMP v1 and v2c on the appliance. Configure SNMP v3 with authentication (SHA-256 minimum) and encryption (AES-128 minimum). Use unique, complex credentials for the SNMP v3 user. Restrict SNMP access to monitoring server IP addresses using access control lists or firewall rules.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Network Management Guide for SNMP v3 configuration.

questions.text: Are firewall rules restrictive and documented?
questions.description: Overly permissive or undocumented host-based firewall rules on the appliance allow unnecessary network services to be accessible from untrusted networks. This is particularly risky for management and monitoring interfaces that should only be reachable from dedicated management networks.
questions.remediation:
Review appliance host-based firewall rules (iptables -L -n -v or nftables list ruleset). Verify that only required services are permitted. Ensure a default-deny policy is in place for all other inbound traffic. Document each firewall rule with a business justification and implement through change management.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Security Hardening Guide for host firewall configuration. Engage Forcepoint TAC before modifying product-related firewall rules.

questions.text: Is configuration backup scheduled and automated?
questions.description: Without scheduled and automated configuration backups, a failed appliance upgrade, hardware failure, or accidental misconfiguration can result in hours or days of manual reconfiguration effort. Critical policy configurations, certificates, and integration settings can be lost permanently.
questions.remediation:
Implement automated configuration backup for the appliance using the built-in export/backup function on a daily schedule. Store backups on a remote server (NFS, SFTP, or S3). Verify that backups include all critical configurations: network settings, product policies, certificates, user accounts, and integration configurations.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Backup and Recovery Guide for your product.

questions.text: Are backups stored in separate location?
questions.description: Backups stored on the same appliance or in the same physical location provide no protection against hardware failure, theft, fire, or ransomware. A backup co-located with the production system will be unavailable at exactly the time it is needed — when the appliance itself has failed.
questions.remediation:
Verify that configuration backups are stored on a separate storage system in a different physical or logical location from the appliance. For cloud-connected environments, consider object storage (S3, Azure Blob) with versioning enabled. Test backup accessibility from the target restore environment.

Forcepoint KB: Ensure backup destination credentials are stored in a secure vault and rotated regularly.

questions.description: A backup that has never been tested is an assumption, not a recovery capability. Backup files can become corrupted, incomplete, or incompatible with a new appliance version without the failure being detected. The first test of a backup cannot be during an actual disaster recovery event.
questions.remediation:
Schedule quarterly backup restoration tests in a non-production environment. For each test, restore the most recent backup to a test appliance and verify that all critical configurations, policies, and integrations are correctly restored. Document test results including restoration time and any errors encountered.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Backup and Recovery Guide for restoration procedures. Include backup restoration tests in the annual disaster recovery exercise programme.

questions.description: Without a defined backup retention policy, old backups accumulate consuming storage, or conversely backups are overwritten before they become useful for rollback or forensic purposes. Compliance frameworks (PCI-DSS, ISO 27001) require defined retention periods for configuration backups of security infrastructure.
questions.remediation:
Define a backup retention policy specifying the number of backup generations to retain (minimum 7 daily, 4 weekly, 12 monthly). Implement automated retention enforcement. Ensure retention periods meet regulatory and internal audit requirements.

Forcepoint KB: Align backup retention with the organisation's data retention policy and applicable regulatory requirements.

questions.description: Backup jobs that complete with errors or that silently stop running go undetected without regular log review. A backup job that has not run for two weeks provides no protection for changes made during that period. Backup failures caused by storage quota exhaustion or credential expiry are common and often silent.
questions.remediation:
Configure backup job alerting to notify the operations team on backup failure or if no backup has been completed within the expected window. Review backup logs weekly to verify successful completion. Integrate backup job status into the NOC monitoring dashboard.

Forcepoint KB: Implement backup monitoring through the backup solution's notification features or integrate backup job status events into the SIEM.

questions.description: Unencrypted backup files containing appliance configuration data expose sensitive information including administrator credentials, integration credentials (LDAP bind passwords, API keys), network architecture details, and security policy configurations. If backup files are stored on accessible storage or transmitted unencrypted, this data can be exfiltrated.
questions.remediation:
Enable encryption for all configuration backup files using AES-256 or equivalent. Store encryption keys separately from the backup files. For backups transmitted over the network, use SFTP, HTTPS, or encrypted storage protocols. Verify that backup files at rest on the storage destination are also encrypted.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the organisation's data protection policy for backup encryption requirements.

questions.description: Without documented disaster recovery procedures for the appliance, an actual recovery scenario will be handled ad-hoc by engineers under stress, using incomplete knowledge, without a validated playbook. Undocumented recovery procedures lead to extended recovery times, missed steps, and potentially failed restorations.
questions.remediation:
Document step-by-step disaster recovery procedures including: hardware procurement/RMA timeline, OS reinstallation steps, product software installation, backup restoration procedure, post-restoration validation tests, and stakeholder notification process. Store documentation in a location accessible without depending on the failed appliance.

Forcepoint KB: Engage Forcepoint Professional Services or TAC to review and validate disaster recovery procedures for your specific appliance configuration.

questions.description: Without SNMP monitoring configured, the NOC/operations team has no automated visibility into appliance health metrics (CPU, memory, disk, interface status, process health). Manual status checks are infrequent and miss transient issues. SNMP is the standard protocol for infrastructure health monitoring and is expected on all production security appliances.
questions.remediation:
Configure SNMP v3 on the appliance. Add the appliance to the organisation's SNMP monitoring platform (Zabbix, PRTG, Nagios, SolarWinds). Configure monitoring for standard MIB-II OIDs (CPU, memory, disk, interface statistics) and any product-specific MIB OIDs published by Forcepoint.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance SNMP MIB documentation for product-specific OIDs. Download Forcepoint MIB files from support.forcepoint.com.

questions.description: Without syslog collection from the appliance, security events, service errors, authentication failures, and configuration changes are only visible through direct console access. This creates operational blind spots, prevents SIEM correlation of appliance events with broader security incidents, and makes forensic investigation significantly more difficult.
questions.remediation:
Configure syslog forwarding from the appliance to the centralised syslog server or SIEM using syslog-ng or rsyslog. Implement TLS-encrypted syslog (RFC 5425) on port 6514 where the SIEM supports it. Verify that all relevant facility/severity combinations are forwarded. Confirm log receipt in the SIEM.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance Logging Configuration Guide and the Forcepoint SIEM Integration Guide for syslog format specifications.

questions.text: Is health monitoring integrated with NOC?
questions.description: Without NOC integration, the operations centre cannot proactively respond to appliance health events. Security appliances not actively monitored by operations staff can fail silently, with degradation only discovered when users report issues or during scheduled audits — by which time significant security events may have been missed.
questions.remediation:
Integrate appliance health monitoring into the NOC's primary monitoring dashboard. Configure escalation workflows so that critical health alerts (service down, resource exhaustion, hardware fault) page the on-call team. Establish a regular health review cadence (daily/weekly) where appliance status is reviewed by the operations team.

Forcepoint KB: Engage the NOC tooling team to integrate Forcepoint appliance SNMP/syslog data into the operations dashboard.

questions.text: Are critical alerts configured and tested?
questions.description: Critical alerts that are configured but never tested may not fire during real events due to misconfigured thresholds, broken alerting paths, or silenced notification channels. An untested alert provides false assurance. Appliance failures should be detected by automated monitoring within minutes, not hours.
questions.remediation:
Test each configured critical alert by simulating or inducing the alert condition in a controlled manner (e.g., manually consuming disk space to trigger a storage alert, temporarily stopping a monitored service). Verify that the alert reaches the intended recipient within the expected timeframe. Document test results.

Forcepoint KB: Include alert testing in the quarterly appliance health review. Maintain an alert test register documenting when each alert type was last successfully tested.

questions.description: Without uptime tracking, SLA compliance for the appliance cannot be measured, recurring availability issues cannot be identified, and business impact assessments of downtime events cannot be quantified. Uptime data is often required for compliance reporting and vendor SLA discussions.
questions.remediation:
Implement uptime monitoring for the appliance using the monitoring platform's availability tracking features. Configure synthetic health checks (ICMP ping, TCP port checks on management and product service ports) to measure availability continuously. Generate monthly uptime reports and compare against the SLA target (typically 99.9%).

Forcepoint KB: Integrate uptime monitoring into the NOC monitoring platform alongside health metrics.

questions.description: Without continuous collection of performance metrics (CPU, memory, disk I/O, network throughput), it is impossible to establish trends, predict capacity exhaustion, or diagnose performance regressions before they impact users. Performance metric gaps make post-incident root cause analysis significantly more difficult.
questions.remediation:
Configure continuous performance metric collection for all key resources using the monitoring platform. Store metrics with at minimum 90-day retention for trend analysis. Generate weekly performance trend reports for the operations team. Configure capacity threshold alerts based on trend analysis.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Appliance SNMP MIB for product-specific performance OIDs. Use a time-series monitoring system (Prometheus, Grafana, Zabbix) for efficient metric storage.

questions.text: Is monitoring dashboard accessible to operations?
questions.description: If the monitoring dashboard for the appliance is not accessible to the operations team — due to access restrictions, lack of training, or tooling gaps — health issues will not be observed in real time. A monitoring dashboard that is not regularly reviewed provides no operational value.
questions.remediation:
Verify that all operations staff responsible for the appliance have access to the monitoring dashboard and are trained on interpreting the displayed metrics. Conduct a quarterly review of dashboard access to remove departed staff and add new team members.

Forcepoint KB: Engage the monitoring platform team to create a dedicated Forcepoint appliance health dashboard view for the NOC.

questions.text: Are monitoring agents up to date?
questions.description: Outdated monitoring agents on the appliance may not correctly monitor newer software versions, may have known bugs causing false or missed alerts, or may be missing support for newer metric types. Stale monitoring agents are a common cause of monitoring coverage gaps that only become apparent during an actual incident.
questions.remediation:
Review the version of all monitoring agents deployed on the appliance (SNMP agent, syslog forwarding agent, metric collection agent). Compare against current versions from the monitoring platform vendor. Update agents during scheduled maintenance windows. Verify that monitoring continues to function correctly after each agent update.

Forcepoint KB: Include monitoring agent version review in the quarterly appliance health check.

questions.text: Is monitoring data retained per compliance requirements?
questions.description: Monitoring data not retained for a sufficient period cannot support post-incident analysis occurring weeks or months after the triggering event. Many security incidents are only discovered long after they began; without historical monitoring data, the timeline and scope cannot be reconstructed. Compliance frameworks often require specific retention periods.
questions.remediation:
Define the monitoring data retention period based on regulatory requirements and incident investigation timelines (minimum 90 days for operational monitoring, 1 year for compliance-related metrics). Configure the monitoring platform to retain data for the required period, archiving older data to cold storage. Verify retention settings and test data retrieval.

Forcepoint KB: Align monitoring data retention with the organisation's data retention policy and applicable regulatory requirements.

questions.text: Are web filtering policies configured correctly?
questions.description: Web filtering policies may be misconfigured, incomplete, or inconsistently applied across users and groups. Improper policy configuration can allow access to malicious, inappropriate, or non-compliant websites, increasing security and productivity risks.
questions.remediation:
Review and validate all web filtering policies to ensure they align with organizational security requirements. Verify category mappings, user/group assignments, exception rules, and policy precedence. Ensure high-risk categories are appropriately restricted and test policy enforcement across different user profiles and traffic scenarios.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to 'How to configure Web Security policies' (Article ID: 000014231) and the Forcepoint Web Security Administrator Guide > Policy Management section for step-by-step policy validation procedures.

questions.text: Is URL categorization database up to date?
questions.description: The URL categorization database is the core reference for all web filtering decisions. An outdated database may fail to classify newly registered malicious domains, phishing URLs, or recently added content categories, leaving users exposed to threats that would otherwise be blocked.
questions.remediation:
Verify that the Forcepoint Master Database is downloading and applying updates successfully. Check the Policy Server and Filtering Service logs for database update errors. Confirm that the update schedule is configured and that outbound connectivity to Forcepoint update servers (downloads.websense.com) is functional on port 443.

Forcepoint KB: 'Troubleshooting database download failures in Forcepoint Web Security' (Article ID: 000010285). Validate update status in TRITON Manager > Status > Alerts.

questions.text: Is malware scanning enabled on downloads?
questions.description: Without active malware scanning on file downloads, malicious executables, scripts, and documents can bypass the proxy and reach endpoints undetected. This is a critical gap in the defence-in-depth posture, particularly for zero-day payloads delivered via HTTP/HTTPS.
questions.remediation:
Enable Content Gateway real-time scanning and ensure the Advanced Malware Detection (AMD) engine is active and licensed. Configure scanning for all relevant MIME types and file extensions. Verify that the scanning engine signatures are up to date and that file size thresholds are not set too high, causing large files to bypass scanning.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring real-time scanning in Forcepoint Web Security Content Gateway' (Article ID: 000012541). Check scanning status under Content Gateway Manager > Configure > Security > Malware Scanning.

questions.description: Failure to block high-risk URL categories such as Botnets, Malicious Websites, Phishing, Anonymous Proxies, and Spyware exposes the organisation to drive-by downloads, credential theft, and command-and-control (C2) communication. These categories are frequently targeted in APT and ransomware campaigns.
questions.remediation:
Review all active policies and confirm that Forcepoint Security Risk categories (Botnets, Keyloggers, Malicious Embedded iFrames, Malicious Websites, Phishing & Other Frauds, Spyware, Anonymous Proxies) are set to Block. Validate that no overly permissive exceptions exist for these categories in any user or group policy.

Forcepoint KB: 'Recommended blocked categories for security hardening' — refer to Forcepoint Web Security Best Practices Guide (available on support.forcepoint.com). Use Policy Risk Score in TRITON Manager to identify policy gaps.

questions.text: Is policy applied consistently across all users?
questions.description: Inconsistent policy application — where some user groups, IP ranges, or endpoints fall into the Default policy instead of the intended granular policy — can create unmonitored or under-protected segments. This commonly occurs when directory synchronisation is misconfigured or when new network ranges are not mapped to any policy.
questions.remediation:
Audit user/group-to-policy mappings in TRITON Manager > Policy Management. Verify that Active Directory synchronisation is pulling all relevant OUs and groups. Review the 'Unfiltered Users' count in Status dashboards; ideally this should be zero or minimal. Ensure that IP-based fallback policies are correctly scoped.

Forcepoint KB: 'How to identify users receiving the Default policy unintentionally' (Article ID: 000013874). Review DC Agent and Logon Agent status to ensure user identity mapping is functioning.

questions.text: Are safe search enforcement rules active?
questions.description: Without Safe Search enforcement, users on major search engines (Google, Bing, YouTube) can access explicit or inappropriate content through search results, bypassing category-level filtering. This is particularly relevant for regulated environments such as education, government, and finance.
questions.remediation:
Enable the Safe Search Enforcement option in Forcepoint Web Security policies. This rewrites search engine requests to include safe search parameters. For HTTPS-based search engines, SSL inspection must be active for rewriting to function. Validate enforcement by testing search results from an affected user account.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring Safe Search enforcement in Forcepoint Web Security' (Article ID: 000011203). Ensure Content Gateway SSL inspection is enabled for google.com, bing.com, and youtube.com to allow rewriting.

questions.text: Is SSL inspection enabled and working?
questions.description: The majority of web traffic is encrypted via HTTPS. Without SSL inspection, the proxy cannot scan content, enforce policies on URLs within HTTPS sessions, detect malware in encrypted downloads, or prevent data exfiltration over encrypted channels. Attackers routinely use HTTPS to evade detection.
questions.remediation:
Confirm that SSL Manager is enabled in Content Gateway and that the SSL CA certificate is deployed to all endpoints via GPO or MDM. Verify that decryption policies are appropriately configured with bypass rules only for genuinely required destinations (e.g., banking, healthcare). Monitor SSL inspection throughput and error rates in Content Gateway Manager.

Forcepoint KB: 'SSL Manager configuration and troubleshooting in Content Gateway' (Article ID: 000010892). Check Content Gateway Manager > Configure > SSL > SSL Manager for current inspection status and certificate deployment.

questions.text: Are SSL certificates trusted by endpoints?
questions.description: If the Content Gateway SSL inspection CA certificate is not trusted by endpoint browsers and operating systems, users will encounter persistent SSL certificate errors, leading to either a poor user experience or — more dangerously — users being trained to click through certificate warnings, undermining overall PKI trust.
questions.remediation:
Deploy the Content Gateway CA certificate to the Trusted Root Certification Authorities store on all managed endpoints via Active Directory Group Policy (Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Public Key Policies > Trusted Root Certification Authorities). For Mac/Linux endpoints, use the appropriate certificate store management tooling. Verify trust status by checking browser certificate chain on a test HTTPS site.

Forcepoint KB: 'How to deploy the Content Gateway CA certificate via GPO' (Article ID: 000011456). Also verify certificate validity period and key length to ensure compatibility with modern browsers.

questions.text: Is SSL inspection bypass list minimal and documented?
questions.description: Overly broad SSL bypass lists negate the security value of SSL inspection by allowing significant volumes of unscanned HTTPS traffic. Undocumented bypasses accumulate over time and become a shadow policy that is difficult to audit. Common targets for attackers include widely bypassed domains such as update services or cloud storage.
questions.remediation:
Audit the SSL bypass (Do Not Decrypt) list in Content Gateway Manager and remove entries that are no longer required or cannot be justified. Each bypass entry should have a documented business reason, an owner, and a review date. Consider using category-based bypasses (e.g., Financial Data and Services) rather than individual domain exceptions where compliance requirements apply.

Forcepoint KB: 'Managing SSL decryption bypass lists in Content Gateway' — refer to the Content Gateway Administrator Guide > SSL Manager > Configuring SSL Bypass. Review bypass list quarterly as part of the change management process.

questions.description: Applications that use certificate pinning (e.g., certain mobile apps, enterprise software, and cloud services) will fail when SSL inspection replaces the server certificate with the proxy's CA-signed certificate. This can cause application breakage that is difficult to diagnose and may result in broad SSL bypass rules being added.
questions.remediation:
Identify applications in the environment that use certificate pinning (common examples: Windows Update, Dropbox, some Google services). Add these destinations to the SSL bypass list using domain or IP-based rules. Work with application vendors to obtain current pinned certificate details and implement application-specific bypass policies rather than broad domain bypasses.

Forcepoint KB: 'Troubleshooting SSL inspection issues with pinned certificate applications' (Article ID: 000013102). Monitor Content Gateway SSL error logs for certificate validation failures that may indicate pinning conflicts.

questions.description: Without Active Directory integration, Forcepoint Web Security cannot map web traffic to individual users or groups, making it impossible to apply user- or group-based policies, generate per-user reports, or perform meaningful DLP or insider threat analysis. Traffic is only identifiable by IP address.
questions.remediation:
Verify that Directory Agent (or DC Agent) is installed, running, and successfully communicating with the Policy Server. Confirm that the LDAP/AD connection is authenticated, that the correct base DN is configured, and that all relevant OUs are included in the synchronisation scope. Restart the Directory Agent service if synchronisation has stalled and review the agent log for errors.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring and troubleshooting Directory Agent for Active Directory integration' (Article ID: 000010341). Verify synchronisation status in TRITON Manager > Settings > Directory Services.

questions.description: If transparent authentication (via DC Agent, Logon Agent, or NTLM) is not functioning correctly, users will receive unexpected authentication prompts, or traffic will fall through to IP-based or unauthenticated policies. This degrades both user experience and policy enforcement granularity.
questions.remediation:
Verify DC Agent is receiving and processing Windows Security Event Log entries (Event IDs 4624, 4768) from all Domain Controllers. Confirm that the Logon Agent (if used) is deployed to endpoints and communicating with Policy Server. Test transparent authentication by logging in with a test domain user and checking real-time traffic monitoring for correct user identity resolution.

Forcepoint KB: 'Troubleshooting transparent user identification with DC Agent and Logon Agent' (Article ID: 000011789). Review DC Agent log at %ProgramFiles%\Websense\Web Security\bin\DCAgent.log for identity mapping errors.

questions.description: Unauthenticated or guest users (e.g., visitors on the corporate WiFi, BYOD devices, contractor endpoints) must be handled by a defined policy rather than falling into an overly permissive Default policy. Uncontrolled guest access can be exploited for anonymous malicious activity or can expose the organisation's IP reputation.
questions.remediation:
Define an explicit Guest or Unauthenticated Users policy in Forcepoint Web Security with appropriate restrictions (e.g., limited category access, no access to internal resources, mandatory captive portal acceptance). Map guest network IP ranges to this policy explicitly. Consider integrating a captive portal solution for guest user identification and acceptable use acknowledgment.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring policies for unauthenticated users and guest networks' — refer to the Forcepoint Web Security Administrator Guide > Managing Clients > Computers and Networks. Review unfiltered user counts in the TRITON Status dashboard.

questions.description: Kerberos and NTLM are the primary explicit proxy authentication mechanisms for domain-joined Windows endpoints. Misconfiguration results in repeated authentication prompts, authentication failures, or fallback to less secure methods. NTLM pass-through failures are a common source of user complaints and help-desk tickets.
questions.remediation:
Verify that the Forcepoint Web Security proxy is correctly registered as a Kerberos Service Principal (SPN) in Active Directory. Confirm that the proxy hostname used by clients matches the SPN. For NTLM, ensure that the proxy is a domain member or has trust relationships configured. Test authentication using a browser configured for explicit proxy with a known domain user and review authentication logs.

Forcepoint KB: 'How to configure Kerberos authentication for explicit proxy in Forcepoint Web Security' (Article ID: 000012034). Review Content Gateway authentication logs at /opt/WCG/logs/squid.log and /opt/WCG/logs/auth.log for Kerberos/NTLM negotiation errors.

questions.text: Are web access logs being retained?
questions.description: If web access logs are not being retained, the organisation loses the ability to investigate security incidents, perform forensic analysis, or demonstrate compliance with regulatory requirements (e.g., KVKK, GDPR, PCI-DSS). Log gaps can make it impossible to reconstruct the sequence of events following a breach.
questions.remediation:
Confirm that Forcepoint Log Server is running and successfully receiving log data from all Filtering Service instances. Verify that the Log Server database (SQL Server) has sufficient storage capacity and that the retention period configured in TRITON Manager > Settings > Reporting > Log Database matches organisational and regulatory requirements.

Forcepoint KB: 'Log Server configuration and troubleshooting guide' (Article ID: 000010567). Review Log Server status in TRITON Manager > Status > Log Server and check Windows Event Viewer on the Log Server host for service errors.

questions.text: Is log retention period compliant with policy?
questions.description: Insufficient log retention periods may result in non-compliance with internal security policies and external regulatory requirements. Many compliance frameworks (PCI-DSS, GDPR, KVKK, ISO 27001) mandate minimum retention periods ranging from 90 days to several years for web access logs.
questions.remediation:
Review the log retention configuration in TRITON Manager > Settings > Reporting > Log Database. Set the retention period to meet the most stringent applicable regulatory requirement (minimum 1 year for most enterprise environments). Consider archiving logs to external storage (NAS, SIEM, or cold storage) before database purge to extend effective retention at lower cost.

Forcepoint KB: 'Managing Log Database size and retention in Forcepoint Web Security' (Article ID: 000011102). Monitor database growth trends to anticipate storage capacity needs before logs are truncated prematurely.

questions.text: Are logs being sent to SIEM?
questions.description: Without SIEM integration, web security events are siloed within the Forcepoint platform and cannot be correlated with events from other security tools (firewalls, endpoint detection, identity platforms). This limits the organisation's ability to detect multi-stage attacks, meet SOAR automation requirements, or satisfy security operations monitoring standards.
questions.remediation:
Configure Forcepoint Web Security to forward logs to the SIEM platform in an appropriate format (CEF, LEEF, or Syslog). Verify that the Log Server or Content Gateway is configured with the correct SIEM destination IP, port, and protocol. Test log flow by generating known test traffic and confirming event receipt in the SIEM console.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring syslog output from Forcepoint Web Security for SIEM integration' (Article ID: 000012780). For CEF output, refer to the Forcepoint Web Security SIEM Integration Guide available on support.forcepoint.com.

questions.description: Insufficient log storage capacity causes Log Server to stop recording events, creating gaps in audit trails and potentially halting filtering operations that depend on log write success. Full disk conditions on the Log Server or SQL Server host are among the most common causes of logging failures in production deployments.
questions.remediation:
Monitor disk utilisation on both the Log Server host and the SQL Server instance hosting the Forcepoint log database. Configure disk usage alerts at 75% and 85% thresholds. Implement automated database maintenance jobs to partition and archive older log data. If the SQL database is on a shared server, ensure Forcepoint has dedicated storage allocation.

Forcepoint KB: 'Log Server stops logging due to disk space issues' (Article ID: 000010943). Review SQL database file growth settings and enable auto-growth with a defined increment rather than using default settings.

questions.text: Is proxy performance meeting SLA requirements?
questions.description: If the proxy is not meeting defined SLA thresholds for latency and throughput, users experience slow browsing, timeouts, and productivity loss. In severe cases, persistent proxy performance degradation leads to IT teams disabling filtering or configuring widespread bypasses, eliminating the security value of the solution.
questions.remediation:
Review Content Gateway performance metrics including transaction rate (requests/sec), average response time, and connection queue depth. Compare against baseline measurements taken at initial deployment. Investigate resource bottlenecks (CPU, memory, disk I/O, network). Consider scaling the proxy (additional nodes in a cluster) or tuning cache and connection pool settings if performance has degraded.

Forcepoint KB: 'Content Gateway performance tuning and troubleshooting guide' (Article ID: 000013421). Review metrics in Content Gateway Manager > Monitor > Performance Statistics and correlate with OS-level resource monitoring.

questions.description: Default or misconfigured connection limits in Content Gateway can result in connection exhaustion under high load, causing proxy failures or request rejections. Conversely, excessively high connection limits can allow resource exhaustion attacks or degrade performance by overwhelming backend servers.
questions.remediation:
Review the max_connections and client_connection parameters in the Content Gateway records.config file. Set limits appropriate to the number of concurrent users and available system resources (RAM, file descriptors). Ensure operating system file descriptor limits (ulimit) are increased to match the configured connection limits. Monitor active connections during peak hours.

Forcepoint KB: 'Tuning Content Gateway connection limits and file descriptor settings' (Article ID: 000011634). Refer to /opt/WCG/config/records.config for connection-related parameters and the Content Gateway Performance Tuning Guide.

questions.description: When caching is disabled or poorly configured, every web request must traverse the full proxy inspection and upstream fetch path, increasing latency and bandwidth consumption. Effective caching significantly reduces upstream bandwidth usage and improves response times for frequently accessed content.
questions.remediation:
Verify that Content Gateway caching is enabled and that the cache disk partition is correctly configured and mounted. Review cache hit ratio in Content Gateway Manager > Monitor > Cache Statistics; a hit ratio below 20-30% may indicate cacheable content is being excluded by misconfigured cache policies. Adjust cache size and object size limits based on traffic patterns.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring and optimising Content Gateway cache performance' — refer to the Content Gateway Administrator Guide > Cache Configuration. Check /opt/WCG/logs/squid.log for cache-related errors (MISS, DENIED, ERR_CACHE_*).

questions.description: Without bandwidth monitoring at the proxy level, the organisation lacks visibility into which users, categories, or applications are consuming the most bandwidth. This prevents effective capacity planning, cost management for WAN links, and identification of anomalous data transfer activity that may indicate exfiltration or compromised endpoints.
questions.remediation:
Enable bandwidth-related reporting in TRITON Manager and configure dashboards to display top consumers by user, category, and destination. Set up scheduled bandwidth utilisation reports for distribution to IT management. Consider configuring bandwidth-based policy actions (e.g., throttling streaming media categories) if specific categories are causing congestion.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to Forcepoint Web Security Reporting Guide > Bandwidth and Data Usage Reports. Review Investigative Reports in TRITON Manager for per-user and per-category bandwidth breakdown.

questions.text: Is the DNS resolution latency consistently below 10 ms?
questions.description: Content Gateway performs DNS lookups for every proxied request. High DNS latency directly translates to increased page load times experienced by users. DNS lookup times above 10 ms per query cause measurable user-facing latency, particularly for pages that load resources from multiple domains. Persistent DNS issues can also cause proxy timeouts and error pages.
questions.remediation:
Configure Content Gateway to use local, high-performance DNS resolvers (internal DNS servers or dedicated DNS appliances) rather than public resolvers. Review the dns_resolvers parameter in records.config. Verify that DNS infrastructure is not overloaded and that negative caching TTLs are appropriate. Monitor DNS response times using Content Gateway built-in diagnostics or network-level DNS monitoring.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring DNS settings for Content Gateway performance optimisation' (Article ID: 000012214). Check /opt/WCG/logs/squid.log for DNS_MISS and DNS timeout entries as indicators of resolver performance issues.

questions.text: Is load balancing configured if needed?
questions.description: In deployments with multiple Content Gateway nodes, the absence of load balancing results in uneven traffic distribution, where some nodes are overloaded while others are underutilised. This reduces overall throughput capacity and creates single points of failure if a heavily loaded node fails.
questions.remediation:
Verify that a load balancer (hardware or software) is distributing proxy traffic across all Content Gateway cluster nodes. Confirm that health checks are configured on the load balancer so failed nodes are automatically removed from the pool. Review cluster membership status in Content Gateway Manager and TRITON Manager to confirm all nodes are active.

Forcepoint KB: 'Deploying Forcepoint Web Security in a clustered Content Gateway configuration' — refer to the Forcepoint Web Security Deployment Guide > Clustering and Load Balancing. Ensure PAC files reference the load balancer VIP rather than individual node IPs.

questions.description: Without DLP integration, web uploads and HTTP/HTTPS POST transactions are not inspected for sensitive data. Users can exfiltrate confidential documents, source code, PII, or financial data through web channels without any detection or blocking. This is a significant data protection gap, particularly for regulated industries.
questions.remediation:
Verify that Forcepoint Web Security is integrated with Forcepoint DLP via the TRITON Manager unified deployment. Confirm that the DLP policy server is reachable from the Content Gateway and that web channel DLP policies are enabled and applied. Test integration by attempting to upload a file containing test-sensitive data and verifying DLP incident generation.

Forcepoint KB: 'Integrating Forcepoint DLP with Forcepoint Web Security for web channel inspection' (Article ID: 000013056). Check DLP integration status in TRITON Manager > Web > Settings > Scanning > Data Loss Prevention.

questions.description: Without CASB integration, the organisation lacks visibility into sanctioned and unsanctioned cloud application usage, cannot enforce access controls for cloud services, and cannot detect risky user behaviour within cloud applications (e.g., bulk downloads from SharePoint, sharing files externally via OneDrive). Shadow IT proliferates when cloud usage is unmonitored.
questions.remediation:
Verify that Forcepoint CASB is integrated with the Web Security proxy for inline cloud application traffic inspection. Confirm that cloud application policies are synchronised and active. Review the cloud application discovery dashboard to identify unsanctioned applications in use and take action to block, limit, or migrate users to sanctioned alternatives.

Forcepoint KB: 'Integrating Forcepoint CASB with Forcepoint Web Security' — refer to the Forcepoint CASB Integration Guide. Check application visibility in TRITON Manager > Web > Reports > Cloud Apps.

questions.text: Are ICAP servers configured and responding?
questions.description: ICAP (Internet Content Adaptation Protocol) integrations extend proxy functionality with third-party content scanning engines (e.g., additional antivirus, data classification, or DLP engines). Non-responsive ICAP servers can cause request failures, timeouts, or complete bypass of the ICAP inspection stage depending on the configured failure mode.
questions.remediation:
Review ICAP server configurations in Content Gateway Manager > Configure > Security > ICAP. Verify that all configured ICAP server endpoints are reachable from the Content Gateway (test with telnet/curl to the ICAP port, typically 1344). Confirm that ICAP server health checks are enabled and that the failure mode (pass-through or block) is set appropriately for each integration.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring ICAP server integration with Content Gateway' (Article ID: 000011987). Review Content Gateway manager logs for ICAP connection timeout or refusal errors.

questions.description: Static malware scanning cannot detect sophisticated zero-day threats and evasive malware that only reveal malicious behaviour during execution. Without sandbox integration (Forcepoint Advanced Malware Detection - AMD), these threats can pass through the proxy undetected. Sandboxing is particularly critical for executable files, office documents with macros, and PDF files received from external sources.
questions.remediation:
Verify that Forcepoint Advanced Malware Detection (AMD) is licensed and enabled within the Web Security deployment. Confirm that Content Gateway is forwarding files to the AMD engine for detonation and that the AMD portal is reachable. Review AMD verdicts in the TRITON Manager reporting dashboard and check for any connectivity or licensing errors.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring Forcepoint Advanced Malware Detection (AMD) integration with Web Security' (Article ID: 000013892). Check AMD integration status in Content Gateway Manager > Configure > Security > Advanced Malware Detection.

questions.description: Third-party threat intelligence feeds (e.g., STIX/TAXII sources, ISACs, commercial threat intel providers) provide additional context and IOCs beyond what is included in the Forcepoint Master Database. Without these feeds, newly identified malicious IPs, domains, and URLs may not be blocked until the next Forcepoint database update cycle.
questions.remediation:
Review the current threat intelligence feed configuration in TRITON Manager. If a threat intelligence platform (TIP) or SIEM is in use, evaluate whether IOC sharing with Forcepoint is configured via the ACE (Advanced Classification Engine) custom category or IP/URL custom block list mechanisms. Forcepoint also supports threat feed integration via the Security Intelligence Exchange (SIX) framework in some deployment models.

Forcepoint KB: 'Adding custom threat intelligence URLs and IPs to Forcepoint Web Security block lists' — refer to the TRITON Manager Administrator Guide > Policy Management > Custom Categories. Contact Forcepoint Professional Services for TIP integration requirements.

questions.text: Is proxy CPU utilization below 70% during peak hours?
questions.description: Sustained CPU utilisation above 70% on Content Gateway nodes during peak traffic periods indicates that the proxy is operating close to its capacity ceiling. This leads to increased request processing latency, queue build-up, and risk of proxy service instability or failure during traffic spikes. SSL inspection and malware scanning are particularly CPU-intensive operations.
questions.remediation:
Identify the primary CPU consumers using OS-level monitoring (top, htop, sar) on the Content Gateway host. If SSL inspection is the primary driver, evaluate whether the bypass list can be expanded for low-risk destinations. Consider adding Content Gateway nodes to the cluster to distribute load. Review the proxy transaction rate and compare against hardware specifications to determine if a hardware upgrade or scaling is required.

Forcepoint KB: 'Content Gateway performance tuning — CPU and process optimisation' (Article ID: 000013421). Monitor using Content Gateway Manager > Monitor > Performance Statistics and implement OS-level monitoring with alerting at 70% sustained CPU threshold.

questions.text: Is memory utilization stable under normal traffic load?
questions.description: Memory leaks or misconfigured memory limits in Content Gateway can lead to gradual memory exhaustion, causing the proxy process to crash, restart, or trigger OOM (Out of Memory) conditions on the host. Unstable memory utilisation results in intermittent proxy outages and unpredictable user-facing errors.
questions.remediation:
Monitor Content Gateway process memory usage over time using OS-level tools (e.g., ps, smem, valgrind in diagnostic mode). Check for monotonically increasing memory usage as an indicator of a memory leak, which may require a patch or service restart. Verify that the proxy_malloc_size parameter in records.config is appropriate for the available system RAM. Review Content Gateway version release notes for known memory-related defects.

Forcepoint KB: 'Troubleshooting Content Gateway memory issues and process crashes' (Article ID: 000012901). If a memory leak is suspected, open a support case with Forcepoint Technical Support and collect Content Gateway diagnostic bundle.

questions.text: Are there any packet drops or retransmissions on proxy interfaces?
questions.description: Packet drops and TCP retransmissions on proxy network interfaces indicate network congestion, NIC driver issues, or hardware faults that degrade proxy performance. Retransmissions increase session latency and can cause browser timeouts, particularly for SSL handshakes where retransmissions extend connection setup time significantly.
questions.remediation:
Use netstat -s, ifconfig, or ethtool to inspect interface error counters on the Content Gateway host. Check for Rx/Tx errors, dropped packets, and overruns. Verify NIC driver versions and firmware. Review switch port error counters for the interfaces connecting Content Gateway to the network. Investigate MTU mismatches or duplex/speed negotiation issues as potential causes.

Forcepoint KB: 'Network troubleshooting for Content Gateway performance issues' — refer to the Content Gateway Troubleshooting Guide > Network Interface Diagnostics. Engage network team to review switch-level port statistics and flow data if host-level statistics appear clean.

questions.text: Are PAC file download and processing times acceptable?
questions.description: If PAC (Proxy Auto-Configuration) file downloads are slow or fail, endpoints fall back to direct internet access, bypassing the proxy entirely. Complex or large PAC files with many conditional rules can also cause significant browser startup delay as the file is parsed and executed for each new connection.
questions.remediation:
Host the PAC file on a highly available, fast internal web server (not the proxy itself). Minimise PAC file complexity by consolidating rules and removing redundant conditions. Use WPAD (Web Proxy Auto-Discovery) where possible to distribute PAC file configuration. Monitor PAC file download times from representative client locations and test fallback behaviour.

Forcepoint KB: 'Best practices for PAC file configuration and hosting in Forcepoint Web Security deployments' — refer to the Forcepoint Web Security Deployment Guide > Client Configuration > PAC Files. Validate PAC file syntax using the pac-validator tool or browser-based validators.

questions.text: Are there any DNS timeout or retry events observed?
questions.description: DNS timeout events in Content Gateway logs indicate that the configured DNS resolvers are unreliable or overloaded. Each DNS timeout forces a retry, doubling or tripling the effective DNS lookup time for affected requests. At high transaction rates, DNS timeouts can cascade into widespread proxy latency and user-visible errors.
questions.remediation:
Review Content Gateway logs (/opt/WCG/logs/squid.log) for DNS_MISS and DNS timeout patterns. Cross-reference with DNS server performance metrics. Add a secondary or tertiary DNS resolver to the Content Gateway configuration for redundancy. Consider deploying a local DNS caching resolver (e.g., Unbound or dnsmasq) on the Content Gateway host to reduce round-trip time and provide local caching.

Forcepoint KB: 'Resolving DNS timeout issues in Content Gateway' (Article ID: 000012214). Review records.config dns_resolvers and dns_lookup_timeout parameters and tune as needed for the environment.

questions.text: Is configuration synchronization working properly across the cluster?
questions.description: In a multi-node Content Gateway cluster, configuration desynchronisation results in inconsistent policy enforcement where different users receive different filtering results depending on which cluster node processes their traffic. This creates security gaps and unpredictable user experience, and makes troubleshooting significantly more difficult.
questions.remediation:
Verify cluster synchronisation status in Content Gateway Manager > Configure > Cluster. Confirm that all cluster nodes are visible and show a synchronised status. Review cluster synchronisation logs for errors. If a node is out of sync, perform a manual push from the primary node. Investigate network connectivity between nodes, as cluster sync operates over specific TCP ports that may be affected by firewall rules.

Forcepoint KB: 'Troubleshooting Content Gateway cluster configuration synchronisation failures' (Article ID: 000013234). Verify that all cluster nodes can communicate on the required cluster management ports (default: 8088, 8089) and that no host-based firewall rules are blocking inter-node traffic.

questions.text: Are any proxy authentication failures being observed?
questions.description: Proxy authentication failures result in users being denied web access or presented with repeated authentication prompts. At scale, widespread authentication failures indicate a systemic issue (e.g., DC Agent failure, Kerberos key expiry, LDAP connectivity loss) that can affect all users simultaneously and generate significant help-desk volume.
questions.remediation:
Review authentication failure events in TRITON Manager > Status > Alerts and in the Content Gateway access logs (/opt/WCG/logs/squid.log — look for 407 Proxy Authentication Required responses). Verify DC Agent connectivity and service status. Check for Kerberos ticket expiry or keytab rotation events. Confirm LDAP/AD connectivity from Policy Server. If NTLM is in use, check that machine accounts are not expired.

Forcepoint KB: 'Diagnosing and resolving proxy authentication failures in Forcepoint Web Security' (Article ID: 000011789). Collect squid.log, auth.log, and DC Agent log entries from the time of failure for diagnostic analysis.

questions.text: Is TLS 1.2/1.3 enforced according to security policy?
questions.description: Allowing deprecated TLS versions (TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1) or SSL 3.0/2.0 exposes users and the organisation to known protocol-level attacks (POODLE, BEAST, DROWN). Regulatory frameworks including PCI-DSS v3.2+ and many national cybersecurity standards explicitly require TLS 1.2 as the minimum protocol version.
questions.remediation:
Configure Content Gateway SSL Manager to enforce TLS 1.2 as the minimum protocol version for both client-facing and server-facing SSL connections. Disable SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1 in the Content Gateway SSL configuration. Verify changes using an SSL protocol testing tool (e.g., testssl.sh or Qualys SSL Labs from outside the inspection boundary) and monitor for client compatibility issues.

Forcepoint KB: 'Enforcing minimum TLS version in Content Gateway SSL inspection' (Article ID: 000014056). Edit SSL protocol settings in Content Gateway Manager > Configure > SSL > SSL Manager > Protocol Settings.

questions.text: Are weak ciphers and protocols disabled?
questions.description: Weak cryptographic ciphers (RC4, DES, 3DES, export-grade ciphers) and insecure protocols enabled on the proxy create vulnerability to known attacks including SWEET32, FREAK, and LOGJAM. These weaknesses can be exploited during SSL/TLS handshake interception to downgrade encryption and potentially decrypt traffic.
questions.remediation:
Review and update the cipher suite configuration in Content Gateway SSL Manager to include only strong, modern ciphers (AES-GCM, CHACHA20-POLY1305) and to explicitly exclude weak ciphers. Use a cipher string such as 'HIGH:!aNULL:!MD5:!RC4:!3DES:!EXPORT' as a baseline. Test the resulting cipher configuration using testssl.sh against the Content Gateway proxy port.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring cipher suites in Content Gateway for SSL hardening' (Article ID: 000013945). Refer to the Content Gateway Administrator Guide > SSL Manager > Cipher Configuration for supported cipher string syntax.

questions.description: QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections), the transport protocol underlying HTTP/3, bypasses traditional TCP-based proxy inspection because it uses UDP port 443. By default, many browsers attempt QUIC connections to supporting servers (Google, Cloudflare, etc.), which may bypass Content Gateway SSL inspection and policy enforcement entirely.
questions.remediation:
Configure the network firewall to block outbound UDP/443 traffic, which forces browsers to fall back to TCP/443 connections that Content Gateway can inspect. Alternatively, implement explicit QUIC/HTTP3 blocking at the proxy level if supported. Monitor for browser-generated Alt-Svc headers that advertise QUIC support and assess the impact of blocking on user experience.
