Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint DLP Reporting Guide > User Behaviour Analysis for repeat violator identification reports.

questions.text: Is user notification configured for incidents?
questions.description: Without automated user notification for DLP incidents, users who trigger policy violations — often unintentionally — receive no feedback about why their action was blocked or flagged. Uninformed users continue to violate policies inadvertently, generating a high volume of repeat low-severity incidents that could be prevented through awareness.
questions.remediation:
Configure automated user notification emails in the Forcepoint DLP console for policy violations. Tailor notification content to explain what was detected, why it is a policy concern, and what the user should do differently. Include a link to the data handling policy. For high-severity incidents, supplement automated notification with manager or HR notification.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring user notification for DLP policy violations in Forcepoint DLP' — refer to the Administrator Guide > Incident Actions > User Notification.

questions.description: Inconsistently applied classification labels — where identical documents receive different labels depending on who classified them or when — undermine the integrity of the DLP programme. Classification inconsistency prevents DLP policies based on labels from being reliably enforced and creates confusion for users about how to handle data.
questions.remediation:
Enable mandatory classification on document creation and modification using the Forcepoint Data Classification (FDC) agent. Configure classification policies that provide users with contextual guidance for their specific content type. Monitor classification distribution in the FDC reporting dashboard to identify categories with abnormal label distributions. Provide regular classification training to users.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Data Classification Administrator Guide for mandatory labelling policy configuration.

questions.description: If automatic classification is not functioning correctly — due to AI model degradation, insufficient training data, connectivity issues with the classification engine, or missing file type support — users receive incorrect classification suggestions. Silent failures in automatic classification go undetected without monitoring.
questions.remediation:
Test automatic classification accuracy using a sample set of documents with known correct classifications. Compare the automatic classification output against the expected result. If accuracy is below 85%, review the classification model training data and consider retraining with additional examples. Check the Forcepoint Data Classification engine health and confirm connectivity between the FDC agent and the classification engine.

Forcepoint KB: 'Testing and improving automatic classification accuracy in Forcepoint Data Classification' — refer to the Forcepoint FDC Administrator Guide.

questions.text: Is classification integrated with DLP policies?
questions.description: If DLP policies do not leverage data classification labels as a policy trigger, the DLP system is missing the most reliable signal available: the classification label applied by the data owner or automatic classification engine. Label-based DLP enforcement is more accurate and has lower false positive rates than content-pattern-based detection alone.
questions.remediation:
Configure Forcepoint DLP policies to use Forcepoint Data Classification labels as a primary detection trigger. For each classification level (Confidential, Restricted), define DLP policies that enforce appropriate channel restrictions based on the label. Verify that label metadata is correctly read by the DLP engine for all supported file formats and applications.

Forcepoint KB: 'Integrating Forcepoint Data Classification labels with Forcepoint DLP policies' — refer to the Forcepoint DLP + FDC Integration Guide.

questions.text: Are classification labels visible to users?
questions.description: Classification labels that are not visible to users in the applications where they work do not change user behaviour and are not used to make informed decisions about data handling. For classification to drive user awareness, labels must be prominently displayed in documents, emails, and in the applications where classified data is created.
questions.remediation:
Verify that classification labels are displayed as visual markings (headers, footers, watermarks) in Microsoft Office documents, PDFs, and emails when Forcepoint Data Classification is used. Confirm label visibility in all applications commonly used to create and share sensitive documents. Test label visibility across different platforms (Windows, macOS, mobile) and applications.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint Data Classification Administrator Guide > Label Visualisation Configuration.

questions.text: How many endpoints are currently protected?
Is Endpoint Agent tamper protection enabled?
Is OCR enabled for image-based content detection?
Are DLP incidents integrated with ticketing systems?

questions.description: Firewall rules that are never reviewed accumulate redundant, overly permissive, or technically broken entries that expand the attack surface and increase rule processing overhead. In Forcepoint NGFW (SMC-managed deployments), rule base review is essential for maintaining both security posture and inspection performance.
questions.remediation:
Schedule a quarterly firewall rule base review using the Forcepoint Security Management Center (SMC) rule analysis tools. Use the SMC's built-in rule usage analytics (hit counts) to identify unused rules. Review rules against the principle of least privilege, change management records, and the current network topology. Document review findings and obtain sign-off from the firewall change authority.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Policy Management > Rule Analysis for rule review procedures.

questions.text: Is rule base optimized for performance?
questions.description: A poorly optimised rule base — with rules ordered suboptimally, containing redundant conditions, or with broadly-matched rules appearing before specific ones — degrades firewall inspection performance. In high-throughput environments, rule base inefficiency can cause measurable latency increases and reduce maximum connections per second.
questions.remediation:
Use the SMC rule analysis tools to identify redundant, shadowed, and overlapping rules. Review rule ordering to ensure the most frequently matched, most specific rules appear earliest in the policy. Consider consolidating multiple rules with the same source/destination/service into fewer rules using group objects. Benchmark throughput before and after optimisation.

Forcepoint KB: 'Forcepoint NGFW rule base optimisation guide' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Policy Optimisation.

questions.text: Are unused rules identified and removed?
questions.description: Unused firewall rules create unnecessary complexity, complicate audits, and represent potential security risks — particularly if they were created for temporary purposes and inadvertently allow access that should no longer be permitted. Accumulation of unused rules is a natural consequence of change management processes that lack a decommissioning step.
questions.remediation:
Use the Forcepoint SMC rule hit count feature to identify rules with zero hits over the past 90 days. For each zero-hit rule, investigate whether it serves a purpose (some rules may be valid but only triggered in specific scenarios). Disable rules before deleting them to confirm no impact. Remove confirmed unused rules through the standard change management process.

Forcepoint KB: 'Using Forcepoint SMC hit counts to identify unused rules' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Policy Analysis Tools.

questions.description: Undocumented firewall rules cannot be safely modified, reviewed for correctness, or defended during security audits. When the original author of a rule is unavailable, rules without documentation must be treated as unknown risk and require time-consuming investigation to assess their purpose and safety.
questions.remediation:
For each firewall rule in the Forcepoint NGFW policy, add a comment or description field documenting: the business justification, the change request reference, the approver, the date created/modified, and the scheduled review date. Implement this as a mandatory step in the firewall change management process going forward.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide for rule comment and documentation field configuration.

questions.text: Are rules following least privilege principle?
questions.description: Firewall rules that violate the least privilege principle — granting broader network access than is required for the specified business purpose — create unnecessary attack paths between network segments. Overly permissive rules are a leading cause of lateral movement success during network intrusions.
questions.remediation:
Review each firewall rule against the stated business requirement. Replace any rules with 'Any' source, destination, or service with specific, scoped values. Segment rules by user group, IP range, and required service. Use the Forcepoint SMC access rights analysis to identify the minimal set of permissions required for each traffic flow.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Access Control Policy for least privilege policy design.

questions.description: Shadowed rules (rules that can never be matched because a preceding rule already matches all traffic in that category) represent unreachable policy intent. When rules are shadowed, the intended security policy is not being enforced — the shadowing rule may be more or less permissive than intended, creating either a security gap or an unintended restriction.
questions.remediation:
Run the Forcepoint SMC policy consistency check or shadow analysis to identify all shadowed rules. For each shadowed rule, determine whether the shadowing rule is correct or whether the intended policy requires reordering. Resolve shadowing by reordering rules or merging conditions. Include shadow analysis in the quarterly rule review process.

Forcepoint KB: 'Forcepoint SMC policy consistency check for shadowed rules' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Policy Analysis.

questions.text: Are temporary rules tracked and removed?
questions.description: Temporary firewall rules created to support specific projects, testing activities, or emergency access requirements that are not tracked and removed persist indefinitely. These rules often grant broader access than is appropriate for permanent production policy and represent a growing security debt.
questions.remediation:
Implement a temporary rule tracking process: all temporary rules must have an expiry date in the rule comment, an associated change request, and a named owner. Configure SMC calendar-based rule activation/deactivation for rules with defined expiry dates. Review rules labelled as temporary monthly and remove any that have exceeded their expiry date.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide for calendar-based rule activation. Include temporary rule review in the monthly firewall operations checklist.

questions.text: Is implicit deny rule at the bottom?
questions.description: The implicit deny rule is the foundational safety net of firewall policy — it ensures that traffic not explicitly permitted by any other rule is blocked. Without an implicit deny at the end of the policy, traffic that does not match any rule may be permitted by default, creating broad unintended access.
questions.remediation:
Verify that the Forcepoint NGFW policy has an implicit or explicit deny-all rule as the final rule in each access control policy. In the Forcepoint NGFW SMC, the implicit deny is configurable at the policy level. Confirm that the implicit deny is logging denied traffic for analysis. Never disable the implicit deny rule.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Access Control Policy > Default Action for implicit deny configuration.

questions.description: Without monitoring rule hit counts, the firewall operations team has no data to support rule base optimisation, cannot identify unused rules, and cannot determine whether traffic patterns have changed in ways that require policy updates. Hit count monitoring is a fundamental firewall management practice.
questions.remediation:
Enable rule hit count collection in the Forcepoint SMC for all active rules. Review hit count data during the quarterly rule review to identify zero-hit rules (candidates for removal) and high-hit rules (candidates for optimisation). Export hit count reports for trend analysis. Use hit count data to justify rule reordering for performance optimisation.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Policy Analysis > Hit Count Reporting.

questions.text: Is change management followed for rules?
questions.description: Firewall rule changes made outside the change management process (emergency changes, ad-hoc modifications, vendor-assisted changes) can introduce security gaps, create undocumented configurations, and cause audit failures. Without change management, the authorised policy and the actual running policy diverge over time.
questions.remediation:
Enforce that all Forcepoint NGFW policy changes are made through the approved change management process: RFC submission, peer review, change advisory board approval, implementation by an authorised engineer, and post-change verification. Configure SMC audit logging to record all policy changes with timestamps and administrator identity. Review the SMC audit log weekly for any changes made outside the CAB process.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Audit Log for change tracking configuration.

questions.text: Is IPS signature database up to date?
questions.description: An outdated IPS signature database means the Forcepoint NGFW cannot detect exploitation attempts for vulnerabilities disclosed after the last update. The gap between vulnerability disclosure and signature availability is typically less than 24 hours for high-severity CVEs; an unupdated IPS database leaves the organisation exposed to actively exploited vulnerabilities.
questions.remediation:
Verify that the Forcepoint NGFW IPS signature database is configured for automatic updates and confirm the last successful update timestamp in the SMC. Check for update errors in the SMC system log. Ensure outbound connectivity from the NGFW management system to Forcepoint update servers on port 443. Enable update frequency to the maximum supported setting (typically hourly).

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring automatic IPS signature updates in Forcepoint NGFW' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > System Updates.

questions.description: Incorrectly configured IPS policies — with the wrong inspection profile applied, signatures disabled, or protection settings misconfigured — can result in the IPS providing minimal protection despite being licensed and enabled. Configuration errors in IPS policies are among the most common causes of IPS ineffectiveness in production deployments.
questions.remediation:
Review the IPS policy configuration in the Forcepoint SMC. Verify that the correct inspection policy is applied to each rule and that the inspection policy includes appropriate signature categories for the protected network segment. Confirm that the inspection policy is active (not in monitoring-only mode) for traffic requiring prevention. Test IPS detection using safe test payloads.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring IPS policies in Forcepoint NGFW' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Inspection Policy Configuration.

questions.text: Is IPS in prevention mode (not just detection)?
questions.description: An IPS operating only in detection mode (generating alerts but not blocking attacks) provides no active protection against exploitation attempts. In most production environments, IPS should be in prevention mode for critical vulnerability signatures to actively block attacks, not merely document them.
questions.remediation:
Review the Forcepoint NGFW IPS inspection policy action settings in the SMC. For high and critical severity signatures, ensure that the configured action is 'Reset' (block and terminate the connection) or 'Block' rather than 'Continue' (alert-only). For signatures with high false positive risk, consider a tuning period in alert mode before switching to prevention. Document the rationale for any detection-only exceptions.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Inspection Policy > Signature Actions for prevention mode configuration.

questions.description: If IPS signatures for critical vulnerabilities (actively exploited CVEs, CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalogue entries) are not enabled, the NGFW provides no protection against the most impactful and widely exploited attack vectors. Signature selection decisions should be informed by the current threat landscape, not only default policy settings.
questions.remediation:
Review the IPS inspection policy in the Forcepoint SMC and ensure that all signatures rated Critical and High are enabled, particularly those corresponding to vulnerabilities listed in the CISA KEV catalogue and Forcepoint Threat Intelligence advisories. Disable only specific signatures that are confirmed to generate false positives in the environment, with documented justification.

Forcepoint KB: Subscribe to Forcepoint Threat Intelligence advisories and cross-reference with enabled signatures in the SMC. Conduct a monthly signature coverage review against the latest CISA KEV catalogue.

questions.description: An incorrectly configured IPS bypass list — allowing too much traffic to bypass IPS inspection — negates the protection provided by the IPS engine. Bypass lists are typically configured for performance reasons (encrypted traffic, trusted internal sources) but can be exploited if the bypass criteria are too broad.
questions.remediation:
Review the IPS bypass configuration in the Forcepoint NGFW policy. Verify that bypass rules are scoped as narrowly as possible: specific source/destination IPs rather than broad CIDR ranges, specific services rather than 'Any'. Ensure that bypassed traffic still undergoes stateful firewall inspection. Periodically re-evaluate whether each bypass is still required.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Inspection Policy > Bypass Configuration. Audit IPS bypasses during the quarterly rule review.

questions.description: IPS alerts that are generated but not reviewed provide no security value. Without regular review of IPS alerts, ongoing attack attempts, reconnaissance activity, or successful exploitation events go undetected. IPS alert fatigue (too many alerts, no prioritisation) is a common cause of alert abandonment in security operations.
questions.remediation:
Configure IPS alert routing to the SIEM for centralised review and correlation. Implement alert prioritisation in the SIEM based on signature severity and destination criticality. Establish a daily IPS alert review process in the SOC. Tune high-volume false positive signatures to reduce alert fatigue. Track IPS alert review SLA compliance monthly.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SIEM Integration Guide for IPS alert forwarding configuration.

questions.description: Deep packet inspection and IPS processing add CPU and latency overhead to traffic inspection. If IPS is causing performance degradation beyond acceptable thresholds, administrators may disable or bypass the IPS to restore performance, eliminating the security benefit entirely. IPS must be sized correctly for the traffic volume and inspection profile.
questions.remediation:
Monitor Forcepoint NGFW CPU and throughput metrics with IPS enabled, comparing against baseline measurements taken before IPS activation. If IPS is consuming more than 20% additional CPU or reducing throughput by more than 10%, evaluate whether the inspection policy can be tuned (disabling low-value signatures, excluding high-volume benign traffic from deep inspection). Consider hardware upgrade if tuning is insufficient.

Forcepoint KB: 'Forcepoint NGFW IPS performance optimisation guide' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Performance Monitoring.

questions.text: Are custom IPS signatures configured if needed?
questions.description: Custom IPS signatures are required when the organisation faces threats from proprietary or industry-specific attack patterns not covered by vendor-supplied signatures. Without the ability to create and deploy custom signatures, the IPS provides no protection against bespoke attacks targeting the organisation's specific technology stack or sector.
questions.remediation:
Evaluate whether the organisation has specific threats (targeted attack campaigns, industrial control system protocols, proprietary application vulnerabilities) that are not covered by Forcepoint's default signature set. If yes, work with Forcepoint Professional Services or the security team to develop and test custom signatures. Establish a review process for custom signatures to ensure they remain accurate and relevant.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Custom Inspection Rules for custom signature development guidance.

questions.description: If automatic IPS signature updates are not enabled, the organisation must rely on manual signature update processes, which introduce update latency and operational overhead. Any gap in the manual update schedule leaves the IPS operating with outdated signatures that cannot detect recent exploitation techniques.
questions.remediation:
Enable automatic signature updates in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC and configure the update frequency to the maximum supported setting. Configure alerting for update failures so the operations team is immediately notified if the automatic update process encounters errors. Test update functionality by verifying the 'Last Updated' timestamp in the SMC matches the expected update frequency.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring automatic signature updates in Forcepoint NGFW SMC' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > System Updates.

questions.description: IPS false positives (legitimate traffic incorrectly identified as attacks) that are not systematically tuned cause legitimate business traffic to be blocked, generate high alert volumes that desensitise the SOC, and may result in the IPS being bypassed or disabled to restore business connectivity. False positive tuning is an ongoing operational requirement.
questions.remediation:
Identify the top false positive-generating IPS signatures in the Forcepoint SMC by reviewing signatures with high event rates and low confirmed-true-positive rates. For each confirmed false positive, apply the minimum necessary exception: source IP exclusion, destination exclusion, or signature tuning. Document each exception with business justification. Review false positive exclusions quarterly.

Forcepoint KB: 'Tuning IPS false positives in Forcepoint NGFW' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Inspection Policy Exceptions.

questions.description: Misconfigured VPN tunnels — incorrect pre-shared keys, mismatched IKE/IPsec parameters, incorrect traffic selectors, or expired certificates — cause tunnel failures that disrupt remote access and site-to-site connectivity. VPN configuration errors are a frequent cause of business continuity incidents in distributed network environments.
questions.remediation:
Review each VPN tunnel configuration in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC against the peer device configuration. Verify IKE phase 1 parameters (encryption, authentication, DH group, lifetime), IKE phase 2 parameters (encryption, authentication, PFS, lifetime), and traffic selectors. Test each tunnel from both directions. Review tunnel logs for negotiation errors.

Forcepoint KB: 'VPN tunnel configuration and troubleshooting in Forcepoint NGFW' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > VPN Configuration.

questions.description: VPN tunnels using outdated encryption algorithms (DES, 3DES, MD5, SHA-1) or short key lengths are vulnerable to cryptographic attacks. 3DES is deprecated for new deployments due to the Sweet32 birthday attack, and SHA-1 is vulnerable to collision attacks. AES-256 with SHA-256 or SHA-384 is the minimum recommended standard.
questions.remediation:
Review all VPN tunnel encryption configurations in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC. Upgrade any tunnels using DES, 3DES, or RC4 encryption to AES-256. Replace MD5 or SHA-1 authentication with SHA-256 or SHA-384. Use Diffie-Hellman Group 14 (2048-bit) or higher for key exchange. Coordinate algorithm upgrades with peer device owners to ensure simultaneous implementation.

Forcepoint KB: 'Forcepoint NGFW recommended VPN encryption standards' — refer to the NGFW Best Practices Guide.

questions.text: Are VPN tunnels monitored for availability?
questions.description: VPN tunnels that are not actively monitored may fail undetected, disrupting remote access or site-to-site connectivity without an alert reaching the operations team. In multi-site deployments, a failed site-to-site tunnel may cut off a branch office from headquarters applications and cause significant business impact.
questions.remediation:
Configure VPN tunnel monitoring in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC to generate alerts when tunnels go down. Integrate tunnel status alerts into the NOC monitoring dashboard. For critical site-to-site tunnels, implement redundant tunnel paths (multiple ISPs) and configure Dead Peer Detection (DPD) to automatically detect and renegotiate failed tunnels.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > VPN Monitoring for tunnel health monitoring configuration.

questions.text: Is remote access VPN configured securely?
questions.description: Remote access VPN configuration that does not enforce strong security controls (MFA, device health checks, split tunnelling controls, idle session timeouts) creates an expanded attack surface. Compromised VPN credentials with weak authentication are the primary initial access vector in many modern ransomware and APT intrusion scenarios.
questions.remediation:
Verify that the remote access VPN configuration requires multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users. Enable device health checks (certificate-based device authentication or endpoint compliance checks). Disable or strictly control split tunnelling. Enforce idle session timeouts (30-60 minutes). Review VPN client connection logs for anomalous access patterns.

Forcepoint KB: 'Securing remote access VPN in Forcepoint NGFW' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Remote Access VPN Security Configuration.

questions.text: Are VPN client software versions current?
questions.description: Outdated VPN client software versions on endpoint devices may contain known vulnerabilities, be incompatible with updated server-side security configurations, or lack features required for security policy compliance (device health checks, modern authentication protocols). Unmanaged VPN client versions create an inconsistent security posture across the remote access user base.
questions.remediation:
Inventory all VPN client versions in use across the remote access user base. Compare against the current supported version released by Forcepoint. Identify users running outdated versions and deploy client updates through the organisation's software distribution system (Intune, SCCM, Jamf). Configure the VPN gateway to reject connections from clients below a minimum version threshold.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW Client documentation for supported client versions and upgrade procedures.

questions.text: Is multi-factor authentication required for VPN?
questions.description: VPN access without multi-factor authentication relies solely on password-based authentication, which is the weakest form of access control. Credential theft (phishing, password spraying, credential stuffing) is trivially exploited against single-factor VPN access. MFA is a mandatory control for remote access in virtually all modern security frameworks.
questions.remediation:
Implement MFA for all remote access VPN connections in the Forcepoint NGFW configuration. Supported MFA options include RADIUS-based OTP (RSA, Duo, TOTP apps), certificate-based client authentication, and SAML integration with an identity provider (Azure AD, Okta). Migrate all users to MFA before enforcing it to prevent business disruption during the rollout.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring multi-factor authentication for remote access VPN in Forcepoint NGFW' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Remote Access VPN > Authentication.

questions.description: VPN logs that are not reviewed provide no visibility into anomalous access patterns, failed authentication attempts, credential stuffing attacks, or unusual data transfer volumes through VPN tunnels. VPN logs are often the first indicator of credential compromise in network intrusion scenarios.
questions.remediation:
Configure VPN log forwarding to the SIEM from the Forcepoint NGFW. Create SIEM detection rules for: failed authentication spikes (potential brute force), successful logins from unusual source geographies, session duration outliers, and data transfer volume anomalies. Review VPN log summaries weekly in the security operations review.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SIEM Integration Guide for VPN log forwarding configuration.

questions.text: Is split tunneling disabled or controlled?
questions.description: Split tunnelling — where VPN clients route only corporate-bound traffic through the VPN while internet traffic routes directly — exposes the corporate network to threats from the user's potentially compromised internet-facing device. Devices browsing the internet directly without enterprise filtering may inadvertently carry malware into the corporate network through the VPN tunnel.
questions.remediation:
Review the split tunnelling configuration for the remote access VPN in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC. If split tunnelling is required for performance reasons, implement a conditional split tunnel that routes all corporate subnets through the VPN while internet traffic is filtered through the corporate proxy or security service edge.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Remote Access VPN > Routing Configuration for split tunnelling options.

questions.description: Without Dead Peer Detection (DPD) configured, VPN gateways cannot detect when a peer has become unreachable due to network failures or device reboots. This leaves stale VPN sessions consuming connection table resources and delays automatic failover to redundant paths, causing unnecessary outage duration.
questions.remediation:
Enable Dead Peer Detection (DPD) on all IKEv1 and IKEv2 VPN configurations in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC. Configure DPD intervals and retry counts appropriate to the link characteristics (typically DPD interval 30 seconds, max retries 3). Verify that DPD is enabled on peer devices as well, and that the DPD parameters are compatible.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > VPN Configuration > Dead Peer Detection.

questions.description: Insufficient VPN capacity causes connection refusals during peak usage periods, preventing remote workers from accessing corporate resources and driving workaround behaviours. VPN capacity planning must account for peak concurrent sessions, not average sessions. Remote work events (weather, public health incidents) can cause sudden spikes to maximum concurrent connections.
questions.remediation:
Review current peak concurrent VPN session counts from the Forcepoint NGFW monitoring. Compare against the licensed session limit and the hardware's rated concurrent session capacity. If peak usage exceeds 75% of capacity, initiate VPN capacity expansion planning. Test maximum concurrent session capacity in a staging environment before reaching production limits.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW Datasheet for your appliance model for VPN session capacity specifications.

questions.description: Undocumented NAT policies create configuration management risks — administrators cannot understand the intent of existing NAT rules, making safe modification impossible. In complex deployments with many NAT rules, undocumented entries regularly cause conflicts that result in incorrect traffic translation.
questions.remediation:
For each NAT rule in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC, add a description documenting: the traffic flow being translated, the business requirement, the change request reference, and the date created. Implement documentation as a mandatory step in the NAT change management process. During the quarterly policy review, add documentation to any undocumented NAT rules found.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > NAT Configuration for description field usage.

questions.description: Source NAT (masquerading) misconfiguration causes traffic to be sourced from an incorrect IP address, which can break application server logging, bypass IP-based access controls, or cause asymmetric routing where return traffic cannot be correctly matched to the originating session.
questions.remediation:
Review all Source NAT rules in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC and verify that each rule is translating source addresses as intended. Test Source NAT behaviour using packet capture (tcpdump) on the downstream server to confirm the expected translated source IP. Verify that the NAT pool addresses are correctly routed back to the NGFW.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > NAT > Source NAT Configuration for policy setup and troubleshooting guidance.

questions.text: Is destination NAT working as expected?
questions.description: Destination NAT (DNAT/port forwarding) misconfiguration causes inbound connections to be directed to incorrect internal servers, potentially exposing the wrong server to external access or causing service availability failures. DNAT errors are particularly impactful for externally-published services.
questions.remediation:
Verify each Destination NAT rule in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC by tracing a test connection from an external source to the published service. Confirm that the connection reaches the correct internal server on the expected port. Review DNAT rules for any rules that publish services more broadly than intended (e.g., allowing all external sources).

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > NAT > Destination NAT Configuration for troubleshooting.

questions.description: NAT pools that are undersized for the number of sessions requiring translation cause SNAT pool exhaustion, resulting in new outbound connections being rejected when all pool IPs are in use. NAT pool exhaustion is a common root cause of outbound connectivity failures in high-session-count environments.
questions.remediation:
Review NAT pool utilisation in the Forcepoint NGFW monitoring. Identify pools approaching utilisation limits (>75% of available IP/port combinations in use during peak hours). Expand NAT pools by adding IP addresses or increasing the port range. Consider implementing Port Address Translation (PAT) overloading with multiple IP addresses for high-volume NAT scenarios.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > NAT Pool Management for pool sizing guidance.

questions.text: Is NAT traversal configured for VPN?
questions.description: Without NAT traversal configured for VPN tunnels, IPsec VPN traffic passing through intermediate NAT devices may be broken or blocked. NAT-T (NAT Traversal, RFC 3947) encapsulates IPsec ESP packets in UDP to allow traversal of NAT gateways. Missing NAT-T configuration is a common cause of VPN tunnel establishment failures.
questions.remediation:
Enable NAT Traversal (NAT-T) in the Forcepoint NGFW VPN configuration for all IKEv1 tunnels that pass through intermediate NAT devices. Verify that UDP port 4500 is permitted through any firewall between VPN peers. For IKEv2, NAT-T is handled automatically. Test VPN connectivity from NAT'd networks to confirm correct operation.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > VPN Configuration > NAT Traversal.

questions.text: Are port forwarding rules minimal and documented?
questions.description: Port forwarding rules that are broader than necessary (allowing access from 'Any' source instead of specific trusted IPs, or publishing services on well-known ports unnecessarily) create unnecessary internet exposure for internal services. Each port forwarding rule is an inbound attack vector that must be scoped to the minimum required access.
questions.remediation:
Review all port forwarding rules in the Forcepoint NGFW policy. For each rule, restrict the source IP/range to the minimum necessary (specific partner IPs, specific cloud service ranges rather than 'Any Internet'). Remove port forwarding rules for services that can be accessed through VPN instead. Document each rule with business justification. Review quarterly.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > NAT > Port Forwarding for rule minimisation guidance.

questions.description: Without NAT logging enabled, network troubleshooting teams cannot trace the pre-NAT and post-NAT addresses for a specific session. NAT log gaps make it impossible to correlate external connection attempts with internal source hosts, complicating both security investigations and network troubleshooting.
questions.remediation:
Enable NAT connection logging in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC policy. Configure log storage to retain NAT logs for at minimum 90 days. Forward NAT logs to the SIEM for correlation with other security event data. Confirm that NAT log entries include pre-NAT and post-NAT addresses and ports.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Logging > NAT Log Configuration.

questions.description: A single Forcepoint NGFW without High Availability configured is a single point of failure for all network segments it protects. Any hardware failure, software crash, or maintenance activity causes a complete network outage. In security-critical environments, NGFW HA is a fundamental availability requirement.
questions.remediation:
Design and implement Forcepoint NGFW High Availability using the SMC HA configuration. For active-standby HA, verify that the standby node is receiving state synchronisation from the active node. For active-active clustering, verify load distribution and session synchronisation. Test failover by simulating an active node failure and measuring failover time.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring High Availability in Forcepoint NGFW' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Cluster and HA Configuration.

questions.description: HA heartbeat and state synchronisation interfaces that share bandwidth with production traffic risk state sync failures under load, causing split-brain conditions where both HA nodes become active simultaneously. Dedicated HA interfaces eliminate this risk and are a Forcepoint NGFW HA design requirement.
questions.remediation:
Verify that the Forcepoint NGFW HA heartbeat and state synchronisation interfaces are dedicated, physically separate from the production traffic interfaces, and connected directly between HA peers (or through a dedicated HA switch). Confirm that HA interface bandwidth is sufficient for the state synchronisation traffic volume.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > HA Configuration > Interface Assignment for dedicated HA interface requirements.

questions.description: State synchronisation failures in an NGFW HA pair mean that the standby node does not have a current copy of the active node's connection table. A failover during a state sync failure causes all active sessions to be dropped, resulting in an outage equivalent to a cold failover. Silent state sync failures are a common cause of unexpected HA impact.
questions.remediation:
Monitor HA state synchronisation status in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC. Configure alerting for state sync failures or state sync lag exceeding acceptable thresholds. Investigate and resolve state sync issues promptly — common causes include HA interface bandwidth saturation, MTU mismatches, and HA interface hardware failures. Test state sync integrity by verifying session table consistency between HA peers.

Forcepoint KB: 'Troubleshooting HA state synchronisation in Forcepoint NGFW' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > HA Troubleshooting.

questions.description: NGFW HA that has never been failover-tested provides false confidence in availability. Failover behaviour under different failure scenarios (active node crash, graceful maintenance failover, network path failure) can differ significantly from expected behaviour if the configuration is not regularly validated through testing.
questions.remediation:
Schedule quarterly HA failover tests during maintenance windows. Test each failover scenario: graceful admin failover, simulated hardware failure (power off active node), and network interface failure. Measure failover time against the RTO requirement. Verify that critical sessions (long-lived TCP sessions, VPN tunnels) survive graceful failover. Document test results.

Forcepoint KB: 'Forcepoint NGFW HA failover testing procedures' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > HA Testing. Include HA failover tests in the annual disaster recovery exercise programme.

questions.description: Without HA monitoring configured, the operations team is not alerted when the HA pair enters a degraded state (standby node unavailable, state sync failed, one node in a failed cluster). An NGFW that appears to be functioning correctly (active node is passing traffic) may be operating without its HA partner for an extended period.
questions.remediation:
Configure SNMP monitoring for HA status in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC. Set up alerts for HA state changes (active/standby transitions, node down, state sync failure). Integrate HA status monitoring into the NOC dashboard. Verify that HA alerts are tested and functional. Include HA status in the daily operations health check.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SNMP MIB documentation for HA status OIDs. Configure SNMP trap receivers in the SMC for HA event notification.

questions.text: Are both nodes at same software version?
questions.description: HA node software version mismatches (where the active and standby nodes are running different software versions) cause state synchronisation failures, policy inconsistencies, and unpredictable failover behaviour. Version mismatches commonly occur when one node is upgraded but the upgrade is not completed on the second node.
questions.remediation:
Verify that both nodes in each Forcepoint NGFW HA pair are running identical software versions using the SMC system inventory. If a version mismatch is discovered, complete the upgrade on the mismatched node during the next maintenance window. Implement an upgrade procedure that requires both nodes to be updated before the change is closed.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW Upgrade Guide for HA upgrade procedures to ensure both nodes are updated correctly and consistently.

questions.description: Split-brain is a critical HA failure mode where both NGFW nodes simultaneously believe they are the active node due to a heartbeat communication failure. Split-brain causes traffic black holes, duplicate NAT translations, and VPN tunnel conflicts. Preventing split-brain requires careful HA interface design and tie-breaking configuration.
questions.remediation:
Verify that the Forcepoint NGFW HA configuration includes a tie-breaking mechanism (priority-based election, dedicated management IP reachability check) that prevents split-brain. Ensure that the HA heartbeat interface has redundant physical paths. Test split-brain prevention by simulating a heartbeat interface failure and verifying that only one node assumes the active role.

Forcepoint KB: 'Preventing split-brain in Forcepoint NGFW HA configurations' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > HA Design Best Practices.

questions.description: Heartbeat intervals that are too long delay detection of active node failure, extending the failover time and the resulting service disruption. Intervals that are too short generate excessive heartbeat traffic and may cause false failovers due to transient network conditions. Correct tuning is essential for optimal HA behaviour.
questions.remediation:
Review the Forcepoint NGFW HA heartbeat interval and dead time configuration in the SMC. Recommended values: heartbeat interval 1 second, dead time 3 seconds for high-availability environments. For WAN-connected HA pairs, increase dead time to account for higher latency. Validate failover timing against the RTO requirement after any heartbeat interval change.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > HA Configuration > Heartbeat Settings.

questions.description: Preemption in NGFW HA causes the higher-priority node to automatically reclaim the active role after recovering from a failure. Without preemption, the standby node remains active after the original active node recovers, which may be the desired behaviour for stability (to avoid a second failover) or undesired if the original active node is preferred for performance reasons.
questions.remediation:
Review the preemption configuration in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC HA settings. Determine whether preemption is desired based on the operational requirements: disable preemption (stable, no automatic re-failover after recovery) or enable with a preemption delay to allow the recovered node to stabilise before reclaiming the active role. Document and test the chosen configuration.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > HA Configuration > Preemption Settings.

questions.description: Without firewall log collection, network security events (connection attempts to blocked ports, traffic from blacklisted IPs, firewall rule matches) are invisible to the security operations team. Firewall logs are essential for network intrusion detection, incident investigation, and compliance evidence.
questions.remediation:
Verify that the Forcepoint NGFW is configured to log all relevant traffic events in the SMC logging policy: allowed connections (for critical segments), denied connections, VPN events, IPS events, and administrator actions. Confirm that logs are being received by the log server and stored correctly. Review log volume against storage capacity.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Logging Configuration for traffic logging policy setup.

questions.text: Is log retention meeting compliance requirements?
questions.description: Firewall log retention periods shorter than regulatory requirements create compliance gaps for frameworks (PCI-DSS, GDPR, ISO 27001, NCA, PDPL) that mandate minimum log retention. Truncated log history also limits the scope of retrospective security investigations.
questions.remediation:
Review the Forcepoint NGFW log retention configuration in the SMC. Ensure that firewall logs are retained for at minimum 1 year for compliance purposes, with higher-risk event categories (denied connections, IPS events, VPN failures) retained longer. Implement log archival to external storage (SIEM, cold storage) before local deletion to extend effective retention.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Log Retention Configuration.

questions.text: Are logs being sent to SIEM?
questions.description: Without SIEM integration, firewall security events cannot be correlated with events from other security controls (endpoint detection, email security, proxy). Siloed firewall logs are reviewed less frequently and cannot trigger automated response playbooks. SIEM integration is a foundational requirement for modern security operations.
questions.remediation:
Configure Forcepoint NGFW log forwarding to the SIEM platform in CEF or syslog format. Verify that the SIEM is correctly parsing Forcepoint NGFW log fields. Create SIEM detection rules for key firewall events (connection to threat-intel IPs, port scan patterns, excessive deny rates). Include NGFW data in the SOC security dashboard.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SIEM Integration Guide for log forwarding configuration and log format specifications.

questions.description: Insufficient log storage capacity causes the log server to stop recording events, creating gaps in the audit trail and compliance evidence. Full disk conditions on the SMC log server are a common cause of logging failures that may go undetected for extended periods, particularly on systems with infrequent operational review.
questions.remediation:
Monitor disk utilisation on the Forcepoint SMC log server. Configure alerting at 75% and 85% disk utilisation thresholds. Implement log partitioning and archival to move older logs to external storage before local disk capacity is reached. Review log retention settings and adjust the balance between retention period and storage growth rate.

Forcepoint KB: 'Log storage capacity management in Forcepoint NGFW SMC' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Log Server Management.

questions.description: Critical firewall events (IPS critical detections, connection to known C2 IPs, firewall service restart, HA failover) that do not generate automated alerts require manual log review to detect. Without automated alerts, critical events may go unnoticed until the next scheduled review, potentially hours or days after the event occurred.
questions.remediation:
Configure alert rules in the Forcepoint SMC or SIEM for critical firewall events: IPS high/critical signature matches, denied connections from internal to internet on high-risk ports, service restart events, and HA state changes. Test each alert by simulating the triggering event. Verify that alerts reach the intended recipients within the expected timeframe.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Alerts and Notifications for alert rule configuration.

questions.description: Firewall logs that are collected but never reviewed provide no security benefit. Regular log review is necessary to identify attack patterns, policy violations, and network anomalies that may not trigger individual automated alerts but are visible in log trend analysis.
questions.remediation:
Establish a regular firewall log review cadence (daily for critical events via SIEM dashboard, weekly for trending analysis, monthly for capacity and anomaly review). Assign responsibility for log review to a named team or individual. Document log review findings and actions taken. Escalate any anomalies identified during review to the incident response team.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Log Viewer documentation for log query and filtering capabilities to support structured log review.

questions.description: Firewall logs that can be modified or deleted by administrators defeat the purpose of audit logging. Tampered logs cannot be relied upon for incident investigation, compliance evidence, or legal proceedings. Log integrity protection is a fundamental requirement of security logging.
questions.remediation:
Configure the Forcepoint NGFW to forward logs to a remote syslog server or SIEM immediately upon generation, so that a tamper-proof copy exists outside the firewall management system. Restrict log deletion capabilities on the SMC log server to a separate, break-glass administrative account. Enable log integrity verification (hash-based) where supported.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Log Security for log integrity and access control configuration.

questions.description: Firewall logs with incorrect timestamps (due to missing or misconfigured NTP) cannot be correlated with events from other systems. Timestamp inaccuracies of even a few minutes can make it impossible to reconstruct attack timelines or match firewall events with endpoint or application logs during forensic investigation.
questions.remediation:
Configure NTP on all Forcepoint NGFW nodes and the SMC management server, pointing to the organisation's authoritative NTP hierarchy. Verify time synchronisation accuracy (within 100ms of the NTP source). Configure alerting for NTP synchronisation failures. Include time synchronisation verification in the monthly appliance health check.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > System Configuration > NTP Settings.

questions.text: Are denied traffic logs being analyzed?
questions.description: Denied traffic logs contain valuable intelligence about attack attempts, misconfigurations, and emerging threat patterns. Without analysis of denied traffic, the organisation misses early indicators of scanning activity, lateral movement attempts, and data exfiltration efforts that were blocked but indicate a compromise in progress.
questions.remediation:
Configure denied traffic logging in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC policy. Forward denied traffic logs to the SIEM and create detection rules for anomalous denied traffic patterns (high deny rates from specific internal IPs, denies on specific external port categories, systematic scanning patterns). Review denied traffic analysis weekly in the SOC security review.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Traffic Logging > Denied Traffic Logging.

questions.description: If the Forcepoint Security Management Center (SMC) is inaccessible, administrators cannot make policy changes, deploy rules, or access logs on managed NGFW nodes. While the NGFW continues to enforce the last deployed policy without SMC connectivity, any emergency policy change required during an incident cannot be implemented.
questions.remediation:
Verify that the Forcepoint SMC is reachable from the administrator management network. Check SMC service health (Server, Log Server, Web Portal) in the SMC console. Ensure that the SMC is running on dedicated, highly available infrastructure with its own backup and monitoring. Configure SMC health monitoring with alerting for service failures.

Forcepoint KB: 'Forcepoint SMC availability and troubleshooting guide' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > System Health. Implement SMC high availability using the SMC HA cluster feature for production environments.

questions.description: Administrative accounts with weak passwords, default credentials, or without MFA are the primary target for credential-based attacks against firewall management systems. Compromised SMC administrator accounts give attackers full control over the firewall policy, enabling complete bypass of all network security controls.
questions.remediation:
Review all administrator accounts in the Forcepoint SMC. Enforce strong password policy (minimum 16 characters, complexity, 90-day rotation). Enable multi-factor authentication for SMC web console access. Remove any unused administrator accounts. Disable or restrict the built-in administrator account where possible. Implement a PAM solution for SMC access.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint SMC Administrator Guide > Administrator Account Security for account hardening guidance.

questions.description: Without role-based access control in the Forcepoint SMC, all administrators have full access to all managed NGFW nodes, policies, and logs. Overly broad SMC access violates the least privilege principle and increases the blast radius of a compromised administrator account.
questions.remediation:
Review the Forcepoint SMC administrator account configuration and assign roles based on job function: read-only for monitoring staff, operator access for network engineers, full administrator for senior security engineers. Restrict which NGFW nodes and policies each administrator can access in the SMC access rights configuration. Review RBAC assignments quarterly.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint SMC Administrator Guide > Role-Based Access Control for RBAC configuration.

questions.text: Are management interfaces on dedicated network?
questions.description: Management interfaces exposed on the same network as production traffic can be accessed by users who have network access to that segment, expanding the attack surface for management system compromise. Dedicated management networks with strict access controls are a fundamental security architecture requirement.
questions.remediation:
Verify that the Forcepoint SMC management interfaces are accessible only from dedicated management network subnets. Confirm that NGFW node management ports are restricted to the management network using host-based firewall rules or firewall policy rules. Implement a jump server or bastion host as the required entry point for all management access.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Deployment Guide > Management Architecture for management network segmentation best practices.

questions.description: Without logging of management access events (SMC logins, policy changes, administrator account modifications), there is no audit trail for privileged actions on the firewall management system. This creates accountability gaps and prevents forensic investigation of administrative actions following a security incident.
questions.remediation:
Verify that the Forcepoint SMC audit log is enabled and recording all administrator login events, policy changes, and configuration modifications. Forward SMC audit logs to the SIEM for centralised review and alerting. Configure alerting for sensitive actions (administrator account creation, policy reset, log deletion). Review the SMC audit log weekly.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint SMC Administrator Guide > Audit Log Configuration.

questions.description: Without automated policy backups, a SMC failure or accidental policy corruption requires manual reconstruction of the firewall policy from documentation — a process that can take days and introduce errors. Automated backups are a fundamental operational requirement for production firewall management systems.
questions.remediation:
Configure automated daily backups of the Forcepoint SMC configuration (including all managed NGFW policies, network objects, and administrator accounts). Store backups on a remote server separate from the SMC. Verify backup completion daily. Test backup restoration quarterly. Include SMC backup in the organisation's disaster recovery procedures.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint SMC Administrator Guide > Backup and Recovery for SMC backup configuration.

questions.description: Firewall policy changes made without following the change control process bypass peer review, testing, and approval steps that catch configuration errors before they impact production. Emergency and out-of-band changes are disproportionately responsible for security-related outages in firewall operations.
questions.remediation:
Enforce that all Forcepoint NGFW policy changes are submitted through the approved change management process (RFC submission, peer review, CAB approval, implementation by authorised engineer, post-change testing and sign-off). Use the SMC audit log to detect and review any changes made outside the approved process. Implement separation of duties — the same person should not approve and implement a change.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Change Management Integration for workflow integration guidance.

questions.text: Are policy deployments tested before production?
questions.description: Policy deployments pushed to production NGFW nodes without prior testing risk introducing blocking rules that disrupt legitimate business traffic or permissive rules that create security gaps. Testing in a non-production environment or using the SMC's policy simulation feature catches errors before they affect users.
questions.remediation:
Implement a policy testing procedure for all non-trivial Forcepoint NGFW policy changes: use the SMC's traffic simulation tool to verify rule matching, test in a staging environment before production deployment, and verify post-deployment connectivity for affected traffic flows. Define rollback procedures before each deployment.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Policy Simulation for pre-deployment testing tools.

questions.text: Is multi-factor authentication required for admins?
questions.description: Without MFA for SMC administrator access, a compromised administrator password provides full control over all managed NGFW nodes. Firewall management systems are high-value targets for attackers because administrator access enables complete bypass of all network security controls.
questions.remediation:
Enable multi-factor authentication for all Forcepoint SMC administrator accounts. Supported MFA options include RADIUS-based OTP, TOTP applications, and SAML integration with an identity provider. Migrate all administrators to MFA before enforcing it. Do not allow password-only authentication exceptions for any administrator account.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint SMC Administrator Guide > Administrator Authentication > MFA Configuration.

questions.description: Administrator sessions in the Forcepoint SMC that do not time out automatically remain vulnerable to takeover if the administrator's workstation is left unattended or if the session is hijacked. Persistent sessions extend the window during which a compromised session can be exploited.
questions.remediation:
Configure session timeout settings in the Forcepoint SMC to automatically terminate idle administrator sessions after 15-30 minutes. Ensure that timeout settings are enforced for both the SMC thick client and the SMC web console. Require re-authentication (including MFA) after session timeout.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint SMC Administrator Guide > Session Management > Timeout Configuration.

questions.text: Is firewall software up to date?
questions.description: Running outdated Forcepoint NGFW software versions exposes the system to known vulnerabilities in the firewall software stack and the underlying operating system. Forcepoint regularly publishes security advisories for NGFW software vulnerabilities; unpatched systems are actively targeted by attackers who use exploit code for publicly disclosed CVEs.
questions.remediation:
Review the current software version on all Forcepoint NGFW nodes and the SMC against the latest release on support.forcepoint.com. Subscribe to Forcepoint Security Advisories to be notified of critical security patches. Plan and implement software upgrades for any NGFW running a version more than one minor release behind the current supported version.

Forcepoint KB: 'Forcepoint NGFW software release and upgrade guide' — refer to the Forcepoint NGFW Release Notes and the Upgrade Guide for your current version.

questions.description: Security patches that are not applied regularly leave the Forcepoint NGFW vulnerable to known exploits. The lag between patch availability and patch deployment is the primary window of opportunity for attackers. Critical security patches for actively exploited vulnerabilities should be applied within days, not weeks.
questions.remediation:
Define a patch management SLA for Forcepoint NGFW: critical security patches applied within 7 days, high patches within 30 days, medium patches within 90 days. Test patches in a non-production environment before production deployment. Maintain a patch deployment log that tracks patch application dates against patch release dates for compliance evidence.

Forcepoint KB: Subscribe to Forcepoint Security Advisories on support.forcepoint.com. Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW Upgrade Guide for each software version for specific upgrade instructions.

questions.text: Is patch testing performed before deployment?
questions.description: Firewall patches applied directly to production without prior testing in a non-production environment risk introducing compatibility issues, behaviour changes, or regressions that disrupt production traffic or management functionality. Production firewall outages caused by untested patches are entirely avoidable.
questions.remediation:
Implement a patch testing procedure for Forcepoint NGFW: deploy each patch to a non-production NGFW node or cluster first, verify all critical traffic flows and management functions, then promote to production during the next scheduled maintenance window. Maintain a test checklist covering all critical capabilities (VPN, IPS, NAT, HA failover) to be validated after each patch.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW Upgrade Guide for pre-upgrade validation and testing recommendations.

questions.description: Without documented update schedules, Forcepoint NGFW software updates are performed ad-hoc, inconsistently, and often delayed until a reactive trigger (a security incident or a critical alert) forces action. Documented schedules create accountability and ensure systematic currency.
questions.remediation:
Create and publish an annual Forcepoint NGFW software update schedule specifying planned maintenance windows for each update cycle. Share the schedule with IT management, operations, and business stakeholders. Review and update the schedule quarterly based on Forcepoint's release cadence and the organisation's operational calendar.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to Forcepoint's product release schedule on support.forcepoint.com for planning update cycles.

questions.text: Is automatic update enabled for signatures?
questions.description: IPS and threat intelligence signature updates that require manual deployment create update latency that leaves the NGFW unable to detect newly disclosed threats between manual updates. Automatic signature updates should be enabled separately from software version updates to ensure continuous protection.
questions.remediation:
Enable automatic IPS signature and threat intelligence updates in the Forcepoint NGFW SMC. Configure the highest available update frequency. Verify that the NGFW and SMC have outbound connectivity to Forcepoint's update servers. Monitor the last successful update timestamp and configure alerting for update failures.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > System Updates > Signature Update Configuration.

questions.description: Forcepoint NGFW hardware or software that has reached End-of-Life will no longer receive security patches, creating an unacceptable security risk. Many regulatory frameworks explicitly prohibit the use of unsupported software in environments handling regulated data. EoL planning must begin at least 12 months before the EoL date.
questions.remediation:
Cross-reference all Forcepoint NGFW hardware models and software versions against the Forcepoint End-of-Life announcements on support.forcepoint.com. For any EoL or EoS products, initiate a hardware/software refresh planning project with a target completion date before the EoL date. Communicate EoL timelines to IT management and procurement.

Forcepoint KB: 'Forcepoint Product End-of-Life Policy' — refer to the EoL announcements page on support.forcepoint.com.

questions.text: Is rollback plan available for updates?
questions.description: Without a defined rollback plan, a problematic NGFW software update cannot be quickly reversed, extending any outage caused by the update. The rollback procedure must be documented, tested, and immediately available to the team performing the update — not developed reactively after a problem occurs.
questions.remediation:
Document a rollback procedure for each Forcepoint NGFW software upgrade: the specific SMC and NGFW version to downgrade to, the configuration backup to restore, the steps to perform the downgrade, and the estimated time required. Test the rollback procedure in a non-production environment. Ensure the rollback procedure is available to the team during the production upgrade window.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW Upgrade Guide for version-specific downgrade procedures and limitations.

questions.description: Without update notifications from Forcepoint, the operations team may not be aware of new software releases, critical security patches, or End-of-Life announcements in a timely manner. Proactive notification is the foundation of an effective patch management programme.
questions.remediation:
Subscribe to Forcepoint Security Advisories and product release notifications on support.forcepoint.com using the subscription management feature. Designate a named individual responsible for monitoring and triaging Forcepoint notifications. Forward critical security advisories to the CISO and security team immediately upon receipt.

Forcepoint KB: Register for Forcepoint Security Advisory notifications at support.forcepoint.com > Notifications.

questions.text: Is maintenance window defined for updates?
questions.description: Without a defined maintenance window for Forcepoint NGFW updates, update deployments are scheduled reactively and may be deferred indefinitely due to availability concerns. The absence of a defined window creates competing priorities between security (apply the patch now) and operations (no change during peak hours).
questions.remediation:
Define recurring monthly maintenance windows for Forcepoint NGFW software updates in the organisation's change management system. Set the window outside peak business hours. Communicate the standard maintenance window to business stakeholders so that expectations for planned downtime are set in advance. Reserve emergency maintenance windows for critical security patches requiring rapid deployment.

Forcepoint KB: Include the NGFW maintenance schedule in the organisation's IT operational calendar and align with the Forcepoint release cadence.

questions.text: Are firmware updates tested in non-production first?
questions.description: Firmware/software updates deployed directly to production NGFW nodes without prior non-production testing risk introducing undocumented behaviour changes or compatibility issues that disrupt production network traffic. Forcepoint NGFW firmware changes can affect traffic handling in ways not always described in release notes.
questions.remediation:
Test Forcepoint NGFW firmware updates on a non-production node or in a lab environment using the same hardware model before production deployment. Validate all critical traffic flows (VPN tunnels, high-priority routing, IPS detection, HA failover) on the test node. Obtain explicit sign-off from the network security team lead before production deployment.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW Upgrade Guide for pre-upgrade testing recommendations and known issues per firmware release.

questions.description: Without application control enabled in the Forcepoint NGFW, the firewall can only filter traffic based on ports and protocols — not on the actual application generating the traffic. Applications that use port 443 (HTTPS) for evasion (tunnelling, application bypass) are invisible to a firewall without application identification capability.
questions.remediation:
Enable application control in the Forcepoint NGFW inspection policy. Configure application-aware rules that restrict or monitor high-risk applications (anonymous VPN apps, P2P clients, remote access tools). Review the application usage statistics in the SMC to identify unexpected application traffic. Create application-based allow/deny rules to replace or supplement port-based rules for high-value traffic flows.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring application control in Forcepoint NGFW' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Application Control Policy.

questions.text: Are geo-blocking rules configured if needed?
questions.description: Without geo-blocking rules for traffic from or to high-risk geographies, the NGFW allows inbound connection attempts from regions with high rates of malicious scanning and exploitation activity. In environments where there is no legitimate business communication with specific geographies, geo-blocking provides a simple and effective risk reduction measure.
questions.remediation:
Identify geographies from which the organisation has no legitimate business communications and that are associated with high rates of malicious activity. Configure Forcepoint NGFW geo-blocking rules to block inbound connections from these geographies on exposed services. Implement geo-blocking with exceptions for known legitimate IPs in blocked geographies (e.g., business partner specific IPs in otherwise blocked regions). Review geo-blocking rules quarterly.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Geo-Blocking Configuration for geographic filtering setup.

questions.description: Without SSL/TLS certificate inspection (deep packet inspection of encrypted traffic) configured in the Forcepoint NGFW, encrypted traffic is not inspected by the IPS engine. Attackers increasingly use HTTPS-based C2 communication, TLS-encrypted exploit payloads, and encrypted exfiltration channels specifically to evade inspection. Uninspected TLS traffic is a significant IPS blind spot.
questions.remediation:
Configure SSL/TLS inspection in the Forcepoint NGFW inspection policy for outbound internet-bound traffic. Deploy the SSL inspection CA certificate to managed endpoints. Configure bypass rules for categories that require privacy (banking, healthcare) or that use certificate pinning. Monitor SSL inspection throughput and CPU impact. Verify inspection effectiveness by confirming that the IPS generates events for encrypted test traffic.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring SSL/TLS inspection in Forcepoint NGFW' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Inspection Policy > TLS Inspection.

questions.description: Without threat intelligence feeds integrated into the Forcepoint NGFW, the firewall cannot block traffic to/from known-malicious IPs, domains, and URLs beyond what is covered by the signature-based IPS. Threat intelligence integration is essential for proactive blocking of C2 infrastructure, phishing domains, and malware distribution sites identified by the threat intelligence community.
questions.remediation:
Configure Forcepoint Threat Intelligence integration in the NGFW SMC to enable blocking of known-malicious IPs and domains from Forcepoint ThreatSeeker Intelligence. For additional threat intelligence coverage, evaluate integration with third-party threat intelligence platforms (MISP, commercial TIPs) via the SMC threat intelligence feed configuration. Verify that threat intelligence updates are occurring at the configured frequency.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > Threat Intelligence Integration for feed configuration.

questions.description: Without anti-malware scanning enabled in the Forcepoint NGFW inspection policy, malware payloads delivered via network protocols (HTTP file downloads, FTP transfers, email attachments via SMTP) are not scanned at the network level. Network-layer anti-malware provides an important defence-in-depth layer complementing endpoint protection.
questions.remediation:
Enable anti-malware scanning in the Forcepoint NGFW inspection policy for relevant traffic types (HTTP, SMTP, FTP). Verify that the anti-malware engine signatures are current. Configure policy actions for malware detections (block and alert). Monitor anti-malware detection rates in the SMC reporting to confirm the engine is actively detecting threats.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring anti-malware scanning in Forcepoint NGFW' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Inspection Policy > Anti-Malware.

questions.description: Without sandboxing capabilities utilised in the Forcepoint NGFW deployment, sophisticated malware that evades static signature-based detection can traverse the firewall and reach endpoints. Sandbox analysis of suspicious files is essential for zero-day threat detection in environments targeted by advanced threat actors.
questions.remediation:
Evaluate Forcepoint's sandboxing integration options for the NGFW (Forcepoint Advanced Malware Detection - AMD, or integration with a third-party sandbox). Configure the NGFW to forward suspicious files to the sandbox for detonation. Review sandbox verdict integration to ensure that files with malicious verdicts are blocked. Monitor sandbox submission rates and verdict statistics.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW AMD Integration Guide for sandboxing configuration. Note that AMD does not support air-gapped environments and requires REST API connectivity to the AMD cloud tenant.

questions.description: Without URL filtering integrated in the Forcepoint NGFW, users browsing the web through the firewall are not protected by URL category-based controls. URL filtering provides protection against known-malicious websites, phishing pages, and malware distribution sites at the network layer, complementing web proxy-based controls.
questions.remediation:
Enable URL filtering in the Forcepoint NGFW policy using the Forcepoint URL Database integration. Configure category-based blocking rules for high-risk categories (Botnets, Malicious Websites, Phishing, Anonymous Proxies, Spyware). Ensure the URL database is configured for automatic updates. Review URL filtering block statistics in the SMC reporting.

Forcepoint KB: Refer to the Forcepoint NGFW SMC Administrator Guide > URL Filtering Configuration for database integration and policy setup.

questions.description: Without active botnet C2 signature detection, connections from compromised endpoints to command-and-control infrastructure pass through the firewall undetected. C2 traffic blocking is one of the most impactful NGFW controls — even if an endpoint is compromised, blocking its C2 connectivity prevents attackers from executing commands, exfiltrating data, and spreading laterally.
questions.remediation:
Verify that botnet C2 detection signatures are enabled and in prevention mode in the Forcepoint NGFW inspection policy. Confirm that the C2 detection signature database is updated automatically. Review C2 detection events in the SMC logs to identify any compromised endpoints communicating with C2 infrastructure. Immediately escalate C2 detection events to the incident response team for endpoint investigation.

Forcepoint KB: 'Configuring botnet C2 detection in Forcepoint NGFW' — refer to the SMC Administrator Guide > Inspection Policy > Botnet and C2 Detection.

questions.description: Without SSL/TLS inspection configured on the VPN, encrypted traffic traversing the VPN tunnel is not inspected by the IPS or anti-malware engines in the Forcepoint NGFW. Malware and C2 traffic using HTTPS or other encrypted protocols inside the VPN tunnel are invisible to security inspection, creating a blind spot in the security architecture.
questions.remediation:
Configure SSL/TLS inspection for VPN tunnel traffic in the Forcepoint NGFW inspection policy. Apply the same SSL inspection profile used for internet-bound traffic to the VPN traffic inspection rule.
